+/*
+ * Copyright (C) 2026 The intel-gpu-macos-driver contributors
+ *
+ * Under the Apache License v2.0 with LLVM Exceptions. See LICENSE.TXT.
+ * SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0 WITH LLVM-exception
+ */
+
+// A stand-in for the part of hwloc's API UMF uses, for macOS builds without
+// hwloc (UMF_HWLOC_STANDIN=ON). macOS has one memory domain and no memory
+// binding (hwloc's own Darwin backend reports one NUMA node and returns ENOSYS
+// from hwloc_set_area_membind), so this describes one NUMA node, os_index 0,
+// with all CPUs and the machine's memory, and binding fails with ENOSYS, which
+// UMF's OS memory provider already ignores.
+
+#ifndef UMF_HWLOC_MACOS_STANDIN_H
+#define UMF_HWLOC_MACOS_STANDIN_H 1
+
+#include <errno.h>
+#include <stdint.h>
+#include <stdio.h>
+#include <stdlib.h>
+#include <string.h>
+#include <sys/sysctl.h>
+
+#ifdef __cplusplus
+extern "C" {
+#endif
+
+#define HWLOC_API_VERSION 0x00020b00
+#define HWLOC_STANDIN_MAX_BITS 64
+
+typedef uint64_t hwloc_uint64_t;
+
+struct hwloc_bitmap_s {
+    uint64_t bits;
+};
+typedef struct hwloc_bitmap_s *hwloc_bitmap_t;
+typedef const struct hwloc_bitmap_s *hwloc_const_bitmap_t;
+typedef hwloc_bitmap_t hwloc_cpuset_t;
+typedef hwloc_bitmap_t hwloc_nodeset_t;
+typedef hwloc_const_bitmap_t hwloc_const_cpuset_t;
+typedef hwloc_const_bitmap_t hwloc_const_nodeset_t;
+
+typedef enum {
+    HWLOC_OBJ_MACHINE,
+    HWLOC_OBJ_PACKAGE,
+    HWLOC_OBJ_CORE,
+    HWLOC_OBJ_PU,
+    HWLOC_OBJ_NUMANODE = 13,
+} hwloc_obj_type_t;
+
+enum hwloc_type_filter_e {
+    HWLOC_TYPE_FILTER_KEEP_ALL = 0,
+    HWLOC_TYPE_FILTER_KEEP_NONE = 1,
+    HWLOC_TYPE_FILTER_KEEP_STRUCTURE = 2,
+    HWLOC_TYPE_FILTER_KEEP_IMPORTANT = 3
+};
+
+typedef enum {
+    HWLOC_MEMBIND_DEFAULT = 0,
+    HWLOC_MEMBIND_FIRSTTOUCH = 1,
+    HWLOC_MEMBIND_BIND = 2,
+    HWLOC_MEMBIND_INTERLEAVE = 3,
+    HWLOC_MEMBIND_WEIGHTED_INTERLEAVE = 5,
+    HWLOC_MEMBIND_NEXTTOUCH = 4,
+    HWLOC_MEMBIND_MIXED = -1
+} hwloc_membind_policy_t;
+
+typedef enum {
+    HWLOC_MEMBIND_PROCESS = (1 << 0),
+    HWLOC_MEMBIND_THREAD = (1 << 1),
+    HWLOC_MEMBIND_STRICT = (1 << 2),
+    HWLOC_MEMBIND_MIGRATE = (1 << 3),
+    HWLOC_MEMBIND_NOCPUBIND = (1 << 4),
+    HWLOC_MEMBIND_BYNODESET = (1 << 5)
+} hwloc_membind_flags_t;
+
+enum hwloc_memattr_id_e {
+    HWLOC_MEMATTR_ID_CAPACITY = 0,
+    HWLOC_MEMATTR_ID_LOCALITY = 1,
+    HWLOC_MEMATTR_ID_BANDWIDTH = 2,
+    HWLOC_MEMATTR_ID_READ_BANDWIDTH = 4,
+    HWLOC_MEMATTR_ID_WRITE_BANDWIDTH = 5,
+    HWLOC_MEMATTR_ID_LATENCY = 3,
+    HWLOC_MEMATTR_ID_READ_LATENCY = 6,
+    HWLOC_MEMATTR_ID_WRITE_LATENCY = 7
+};
+typedef unsigned hwloc_memattr_id_t;
+
+struct hwloc_numanode_attr_s {
+    hwloc_uint64_t local_memory;
+    unsigned page_types_len;
+    void *page_types;
+};
+union hwloc_obj_attr_u {
+    struct hwloc_numanode_attr_s numanode;
+};
+
+struct hwloc_obj {
+    hwloc_obj_type_t type;
+    unsigned os_index;
+    unsigned logical_index;
+    union hwloc_obj_attr_u *attr;
+    hwloc_cpuset_t cpuset;
+    hwloc_nodeset_t nodeset;
+};
+typedef struct hwloc_obj *hwloc_obj_t;
+
+struct hwloc_location {
+    enum hwloc_location_type_e {
+        HWLOC_LOCATION_TYPE_OBJECT = 0,
+        HWLOC_LOCATION_TYPE_CPUSET = 1
+    } type;
+    union hwloc_location_u {
+        hwloc_cpuset_t cpuset;
+        hwloc_obj_t object;
+    } location;
+};
+
+struct hwloc_topology {
+    struct hwloc_bitmap_s cpuset;
+    struct hwloc_bitmap_s nodeset;
+    union hwloc_obj_attr_u attr;
+    struct hwloc_obj node;
+};
+typedef struct hwloc_topology *hwloc_topology_t;
+
+/* bitmaps (64 bits: CPUs beyond 64 are not represented; only node 0 is) */
+static inline hwloc_bitmap_t hwloc_bitmap_alloc(void) {
+    return (hwloc_bitmap_t)calloc(1, sizeof(struct hwloc_bitmap_s));
+}
+static inline void hwloc_bitmap_free(hwloc_bitmap_t b) { free(b); }
+static inline hwloc_bitmap_t hwloc_bitmap_dup(hwloc_const_bitmap_t b) {
+    hwloc_bitmap_t d = hwloc_bitmap_alloc();
+    if (d && b) {
+        d->bits = b->bits;
+    }
+    return d;
+}
+static inline void hwloc_bitmap_zero(hwloc_bitmap_t b) { b->bits = 0; }
+static inline int hwloc_bitmap_set(hwloc_bitmap_t b, unsigned i) {
+    if (i >= HWLOC_STANDIN_MAX_BITS) {
+        errno = EINVAL;
+        return -1;
+    }
+    b->bits |= (uint64_t)1 << i;
+    return 0;
+}
+static inline int hwloc_bitmap_or(hwloc_bitmap_t r, hwloc_const_bitmap_t a,
+                                  hwloc_const_bitmap_t b) {
+    r->bits = a->bits | b->bits;
+    return 0;
+}
+static inline int hwloc_bitmap_intersects(hwloc_const_bitmap_t a,
+                                          hwloc_const_bitmap_t b) {
+    return (a->bits & b->bits) != 0;
+}
+static inline int hwloc_bitmap_list_snprintf(char *buf, size_t len,
+                                             hwloc_const_bitmap_t b) {
+    size_t n = 0;
+    int first = 1;
+    if (len) {
+        buf[0] = '\0';
+    }
+    for (unsigned i = 0; i < HWLOC_STANDIN_MAX_BITS; i++) {
+        if (!(b->bits & ((uint64_t)1 << i))) {
+            continue;
+        }
+        int w = snprintf(buf + (n < len ? n : len), n < len ? len - n : 0,
+                         first ? "%u" : ",%u", i);
+        if (w < 0) {
+            return -1;
+        }
+        n += (size_t)w;
+        first = 0;
+    }
+    return (int)n;
+}
+
+/* topology: one machine, one NUMA node (os_index 0) with every CPU */
+static inline int hwloc_topology_init(hwloc_topology_t *t) {
+    *t = (hwloc_topology_t)calloc(1, sizeof(struct hwloc_topology));
+    return *t ? 0 : -1;
+}
+static inline int
+hwloc_topology_set_all_types_filter(hwloc_topology_t t,
+                                    enum hwloc_type_filter_e f) {
+    (void)t;
+    (void)f;
+    return 0;
+}
+static inline int hwloc_topology_load(hwloc_topology_t t) {
+    int ncpu = 1;
+    uint64_t mem = 0;
+    size_t sz = sizeof(ncpu);
+    if (sysctlbyname("hw.logicalcpu", &ncpu, &sz, NULL, 0) || ncpu < 1) {
+        ncpu = 1;
+    }
+    sz = sizeof(mem);
+    if (sysctlbyname("hw.memsize", &mem, &sz, NULL, 0)) {
+        mem = 0;
+    }
+    t->cpuset.bits = ncpu >= HWLOC_STANDIN_MAX_BITS
+                         ? ~(uint64_t)0
+                         : (((uint64_t)1 << ncpu) - 1);
+    t->nodeset.bits = 1;
+    t->attr.numanode.local_memory = mem;
+    t->node.type = HWLOC_OBJ_NUMANODE;
+    t->node.os_index = 0;
+    t->node.logical_index = 0;
+    t->node.attr = &t->attr;
+    t->node.cpuset = &t->cpuset;
+    t->node.nodeset = &t->nodeset;
+    return 0;
+}
+static inline void hwloc_topology_destroy(hwloc_topology_t t) { free(t); }
+static inline hwloc_const_nodeset_t
+hwloc_topology_get_complete_nodeset(hwloc_topology_t t) {
+    return &t->nodeset;
+}
+static inline int hwloc_get_nbobjs_by_type(hwloc_topology_t t,
+                                           hwloc_obj_type_t type) {
+    (void)t;
+    return type == HWLOC_OBJ_NUMANODE ? 1 : 0;
+}
+static inline hwloc_obj_t hwloc_get_next_obj_by_type(hwloc_topology_t t,
+                                                     hwloc_obj_type_t type,
+                                                     hwloc_obj_t prev) {
+    return (type == HWLOC_OBJ_NUMANODE && prev == NULL) ? &t->node : NULL;
+}
+static inline hwloc_obj_t
+hwloc_get_numanode_obj_by_os_index(hwloc_topology_t t, unsigned os_index) {
+    return os_index == 0 ? &t->node : NULL;
+}
+
+/* memory binding: not available on macOS (as in hwloc's Darwin backend) */
+static inline int hwloc_set_area_membind(hwloc_topology_t t, const void *addr,
+                                         size_t len, hwloc_const_bitmap_t set,
+                                         hwloc_membind_policy_t policy,
+                                         int flags) {
+    (void)t;
+    (void)addr;
+    (void)len;
+    (void)set;
+    (void)policy;
+    (void)flags;
+    errno = ENOSYS;
+    return -1;
+}
+static inline int hwloc_get_area_memlocation(hwloc_topology_t t,
+                                             const void *addr, size_t len,
+                                             hwloc_bitmap_t set, int flags) {
+    (void)t;
+    (void)addr;
+    (void)len;
+    (void)flags;
+    set->bits = 1;
+    return 0;
+}
+static inline int hwloc_memattr_get_value(hwloc_topology_t t,
+                                          hwloc_memattr_id_t attribute,
+                                          hwloc_obj_t target,
+                                          struct hwloc_location *initiator,
+                                          unsigned long flags,
+                                          hwloc_uint64_t *value) {
+    (void)t;
+    (void)attribute;
+    (void)target;
+    (void)initiator;
+    (void)flags;
+    (void)value;
+    errno = ENOENT;
+    return -1;
+}
+
+#ifdef __cplusplus
+}
+#endif
+
+#endif /* UMF_HWLOC_MACOS_STANDIN_H */
--

# Türkçe terimler sözlüğü

Proje sitesinin (site/), Türkçe kurulum rehberinin (release/templates/README-INSTALL.tr.md) ve diğer Türkçe
belgelerin kullandığı terimler. Amaç, aynı kavramın her sayfada aynı sözcükle geçmesi ve çevirinin İngilizceden
sözcük sözcük aktarılmış gibi değil, doğal Türkçe gibi okunması.

## Genel kural

- **Ekranda İngilizce görünen ne varsa İngilizce kalır:** firmware (BIOS/UEFI) menü öğeleri, OpenCore'un ve
  config.plist'in anahtarları, komutlar, dosya ve klasör adları, ürün adları, OpenCore açılış menüsündeki öğeler.
  Kullanıcı bunları ekranda o hâliyle arayacak.
- **macOS'un kendi arayüz adları, macOS Türkçe kullanıldığında gösterdiği adla yazılır** (Sistem Ayarları,
  Bu Mac Hakkında...). Rehberi okuyan kişi büyük olasılıkla macOS'u Türkçe kullanıyor.
- **IntelXe Manager'ın (macOS ve Windows) düğme ve sayfa adları, uygulamanın Türkçe arayüzündeki adlarıyla yazılır**
  (app/Resources/tr.lproj/Localizable.strings, windows/app/IntelXe.App/Strings/tr-TR/Resources.resw). Ekran
  görüntüleri İngilizce arayüzden olduğu için gerekirse İngilizce adı ayraç içinde eklenir.
- **Kavramlar Türkçeleştirilir**, sitenin zaten en çok kullandığı karşılıkla. Türkçe hackintosh kullanıcılarının
  yerleşik olarak İngilizce söylediği birkaç terim (kext, quirk, boot-arg, firmware) İngilizce kalır.
- Okura her yerde **"siz"** diye seslenilir.

## Kesme işareti ve ekler

Ek, adın okunuşuna göre gelir; kod biçimindeki adlarda kesme işareti `</code>`'dan hemen sonra yazılır.

| Ad | Okunuş | Örnekler |
|---|---|---|
| macOS | mek-o-es | macOS'u, macOS'ta, macOS'tan, macOS'un |
| EFI | efi | EFI'yi, EFI'de, EFI'den, EFI'nin, EFI'si |
| install.sh, efi.sh, hidpi.sh | ...eş | install.sh'i, install.sh'in, install.sh'e, install.sh'te (install.sh'nin değil) |
| .kext, .plist, .ps1 | kekst, pi-list, pe-es-bir | IntelXe.kext'i, config.plist'te, IntelXe-EFI.ps1'i |
| .aml | a-em-el | SSDT-ARCOFF.aml'i, SSDT-ARCOFF.aml'in |
| .bundle | bandıl | NVMTLDriver.bundle'ı, NVMTLDriver.bundle'da |
| /Library | laybrıri | /Library'ye, /Library'de, /Library'deki |
| SIP, AMFI | sip, amfi | SIP'i, SIP'in; AMFI'yi, AMFI'nin |
| GPU | ge-pe-u | GPU'yu, GPU'nun, GPU'da |

# Licensing

**This repository is public and noncommercial.** It mixes our own MIT code with nullmoth's code under the PolyForm Noncommercial License 1.0.0. That licence lets anyone use, change and distribute the nullmoth parts (the Metal plugin, NMXAccel, NMXAGDC and IntelXeFB) for any noncommercial purpose, provided every copy carries the licence terms (or their URL) and the `Required Notice:` line; this repository and its release packages do both. Any product that contains the nullmoth parts may therefore be used and shared only for noncommercial purposes; commercial use would need the licensor's permission.

| Path | Licence | Notes |
|---|---|---|

| `kernel/IntelXe/uapi/` | MIT (`intelxe_drm.h`, ours). `xe_drm.h`, `drm.h`, `drm_mode.h`: Linux/Mesa uAPI headers under their own MIT-style notices | |
| `kernel/IntelXeFB/IntelXeFB.cpp` | **PolyForm Noncommercial 1.0.0** | derived from nullmoth NMIntelFB/NVRMFB; Required Notice in the file and in `kernel/IntelXeFB/LICENSE` |
| `kernel/IntelXeFB/IntelXeLink.cpp`, `IntelXeLink.h` | MIT | `IntelXeLink.cpp` contains i915 display material (intel_cx0_phy.c, intel_ddi_buf_trans.c; MIT, © Intel, full notice in the file) |

## Build dependencies (not in this repository)

- **MacKernelSDK** (acidanthera, **APSL-2.0**): kernel headers and `libkmod.a`, used to build the kexts. Not vendored; `build.py --sdk`, `MACKERNELSDK`, or `external/MacKernelSDK`. The kexts link `libkmod.a` from it.
- **Lilu** (acidanthera, **BSD-3-Clause**): headers and `plugin_start.cpp` for HybridPM. Not vendored; `kernel/HybridPM/build.py --lilu`, `LILU`, or `external/Lilu.kext`.
- **Mesa source tree:** patched with `mesa/` (MIT and the licences above). It also provides the Vulkan headers for the plugin and the tests.
- **FFmpeg 9.0.2 source:** for the VideoToolbox codecs' shared libraries (LGPL-2.1-or-later), patched by `videotoolbox/ffmpeg/apply-patches.sh` and configured by `videotoolbox/ffmpeg/configure-shared.sh`.
- **Vulkan-Loader / Vulkan-Tools** (`vulkan-sdk-1.4.363.0`, Apache-2.0): optional, for ordinary Vulkan apps (`user/vulkan-loader/`).
- **Rust toolchain and crates:** for the translator. The crates' licences are listed in its `Cargo.lock` dependency graph (MIT/Apache-2.0 in the main).
- **linux-firmware:** `bmg_guc_70.bin`, `bmg_huc.bin` (`LICENSE.xe`); XeProbe's `lnl_guc_70.bin`, `ptl_guc_70.bin` (`LICENSE.xe`) and `tgl`/`adlp`/`dg1`/`dg2`/`mtl_guc_70.bin` (`LICENSE.i915`).
- **nullmoth 2.1.0 release package:** only the air-runtime (LLVM/zstd) is taken from it. The decoder program the plugin runs
  beside it (`nvmtl-air-dis`) is built from this repository's source.

## Not part of this repository

- Remote-access tooling of the test setup is not part of the repository and is not referenced by the build.
- No machine secrets: no ACPI tables with serials (e.g. `MSDM.aml`), no keys, no NVRAM dumps. `efi/` holds notes and the source of `SSDT-ARCOFF` only.
- The GuC/HuC firmware, MacKernelSDK, Mesa, FFmpeg and the Vulkan loader are fetched or built separately (see above).

# Quick start: the IntelXe Manager way

[Türkçe](QUICKSTART.tr.md)

One page for the usual case: a PC with an Arc B580 or B570 that boots macOS with OpenCore, set up with the
**IntelXe Manager** app. Each step names the section of the full guide,
[`release/README-INSTALL.md`](../release/README-INSTALL.md), that explains it, gives the Terminal commands and says what
to do when something goes wrong.

Experimental and unsigned: read the warning at the top of the full guide first.

## Before you start

- **A USB stick with a working OpenCore EFI**, and your firmware's boot-menu key. If the PC does not come up after a
  change, you boot from the stick.
- **One monitor on the card's DisplayPort.**
- macOS 26 Tahoe or 15 Sequoia, installed with a plain OpenCore EFI ([Dortania's guide](https://dortania.github.io/OpenCore-Install-Guide/);
  full guide, stage 1). The screen is slow until the end: macOS runs on the card's firmware output.
- No `IntelXe.kext` or `SSDT-ARCOFF.aml` in the EFI yet. They come last (step 5).

## 1. Get the app

Download `IntelXe-Manager-<version>.zip` from the [releases page](https://github.com/yusufklncc/intel-gpu-macos-driver/releases)
into Downloads, then in Terminal:

```sh
mkdir -p ~/Applications && ditto -x -k ~/Downloads/IntelXe-Manager-*.zip ~/Applications
xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine ~/Applications/"IntelXe Manager.app"
open ~/Applications/"IntelXe Manager.app"
```

The second line is needed because the app is not signed with an Apple developer ID (full guide, 3.1).

<p align="center"><img src="images/manager-overview.png" width="70%" alt="IntelXe Manager's Overview page with the driver working"></p>

## 2. The setup assistant opens

On its first start the app shows its setup assistant. It does the steps below one page at a time, shows what each
change will be before it asks for your password, and continues where it stopped when you open the app again after a
restart.

## 3. Prepare OpenCore (stage 2)

The assistant changes OpenCore's `config.plist` in the EFI you booted from: relaxed SIP, the AMFI boot-arg, two quirks
and one console setting. Tick *Also prepare Safari on the GPU* if you want Safari on the card later. It backs up the
whole EFI folder first. When OpenCore did not record which EFI it booted from, the app lists the EFI partitions to
choose from.

**Restart**, then open the app again.

Preparing the EFI from Windows instead: IntelXe Manager for Windows (`IntelXeManager-VERSION-win-x64.zip`, from
0.1.5), or `IntelXe-EFI.ps1` in the `-efi.zip` as a script (full guide, *On Windows* and stage 2).

## 4. Install the driver (stage 3)

The assistant downloads the package for your macOS, checks the release's signature and the package's checksum, and
installs it. It
backs up what it replaces and can undo it.

**Do not restart yet.**

## 5. The EFI (stage 4)

The assistant adds `IntelXe.kext` and `SSDT-ARCOFF.aml` to the EFI. It rewrites the table for your card's ACPI path when
it is not the shipped one. On a 12th-14th gen Intel CPU with E-cores it also adds `HybridPM.kext` below `Lilu.kext`;
HybridPM needs Lilu, which this project does not ship (full guide, *Hybrid Intel CPUs*).

**Restart.** The desktop should now move at your monitor's refresh rate.

## 6. Check

- The app's Overview page says the driver is working, and About This Mac names the card.
- The assistant's last page runs a GPU test and offers the extras: Safari on the GPU (the system-volume copy; full
  guide, 3.3), OpenGL through Zink for Minecraft Java and other LWJGL games, HiDPI modes, a menu bar item.

## If it does not come up

Boot from the USB stick, or press Shift with the OpenCore entry selected for safe mode, and undo the driver
(`sudo ./install.sh --undo` in the package, or the app's Driver page). The full guide's *If it does not come up* has
the details, and *Reporting a problem* says how to make a diagnostics report.

## Later releases

The app's Driver page downloads and installs a new release over the old one; then its EFI page replaces
`IntelXe.kext` (full guide, *Upgrading*). The release notes say when a step is needed.

# Hızlı başlangıç: IntelXe Manager ile

[English](QUICKSTART.md)

Olağan durum için tek sayfa: Arc B580 ya da B570 takılı, macOS'u OpenCore ile açan bir PC; kurulum **IntelXe
Manager** uygulamasıyla yapılıyor. Her adım, tam kılavuzda ([`release/README-INSTALL.tr.md`](../release/README-INSTALL.tr.md))
onu anlatan bölümü söylüyor; Terminal komutları ve bir şey ters giderse ne yapılacağı orada.

Deneysel ve imzasız: önce tam kılavuzun başındaki uyarıyı okuyun.

## Başlamadan önce

- **Çalışan bir OpenCore EFI'si olan bir USB bellek** ve anakartınızın açılış menüsü tuşu. Bir değişiklikten sonra PC
  açılmazsa bellekten açarsınız.
- **Kartın DisplayPort çıkışına bağlı tek monitör.**
- Sade bir OpenCore EFI'siyle kurulmuş macOS 26 Tahoe ya da 15 Sequoia ([Dortania kılavuzu](https://dortania.github.io/OpenCore-Install-Guide/);
  tam kılavuz, 1. aşama). Ekran sona kadar yavaş: macOS kartın firmware çıkışında çalışıyor.
- EFI'de henüz `IntelXe.kext` ya da `SSDT-ARCOFF.aml` olmamalı. Onlar en sonda geliyor (5. adım).

## 1. Uygulamayı indirin

[Sürümler sayfasından](https://github.com/yusufklncc/intel-gpu-macos-driver/releases) `IntelXe-Manager-<sürüm>.zip`
dosyasını İndirilenler'e indirin, sonra Terminal'de:

```sh
mkdir -p ~/Applications && ditto -x -k ~/Downloads/IntelXe-Manager-*.zip ~/Applications
xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine ~/Applications/"IntelXe Manager.app"
open ~/Applications/"IntelXe Manager.app"
```

İkinci satır gerekli, çünkü uygulama bir Apple geliştirici kimliğiyle imzalı değil (tam kılavuz, 3.1).

<p align="center"><img src="images/manager-overview.png" width="70%" alt="IntelXe Manager'ın sürücünün çalıştığını gösteren Genel bakış sayfası"></p>

## 2. Kurulum yardımcısı açılır

Uygulama ilk açılışta kurulum yardımcısını gösterir. Aşağıdaki adımları sayfa sayfa yapar, parolanızı sormadan önce
her değişikliğin ne olacağını gösterir ve yeniden başlattıktan sonra uygulamayı açtığınızda kaldığı yerden devam eder.

## 3. OpenCore'u hazırlayın (2. aşama)

Yardımcı, açtığınız EFI'deki OpenCore `config.plist` dosyasını değiştirir: gevşetilmiş SIP, AMFI boot-arg'ı, iki quirk
ve bir konsol ayarı. Safari'yi sonra kartta çalıştırmak istiyorsanız *Safari'yi de GPU için hazırla* seçeneğini
işaretleyin. Önce bütün EFI klasörünü yedekler. OpenCore hangi EFI'den açıldığını kaydetmediyse uygulama seçmeniz için
EFI bölümlerini listeler.

**Yeniden başlatın**, sonra uygulamayı yeniden açın.

EFI'yi bunun yerine Windows'tan hazırlamak için: Windows için IntelXe Manager (`IntelXeManager-SÜRÜM-win-x64.zip`,
0.1.5'ten itibaren) ya da betik olarak `-efi.zip` içindeki `IntelXe-EFI.ps1` (tam kılavuz, *Windows'ta* ve 2. aşama).

## 4. Sürücüyü kurun (3. aşama)

Yardımcı macOS sürümünüze uygun paketi indirir, sürümün imzasını ve paketin sağlama toplamını denetler ve kurar. Değiştirdiklerini
yedekler ve kurulumu geri alabilir.

**Henüz yeniden başlatmayın.**

## 5. EFI (4. aşama)

Yardımcı EFI'ye `IntelXe.kext` ve `SSDT-ARCOFF.aml` ekler. Kartınızın ACPI yolu paketteki tablonunkinden farklıysa
tabloyu ona göre yeniden yazar. E-çekirdekli 12.-14. nesil bir Intel işlemcide `HybridPM.kext`'i de `Lilu.kext`'in
altına ekler; HybridPM, bu projenin dağıtmadığı Lilu'ya ihtiyaç duyar (tam kılavuz, *Hibrit Intel işlemciler*).

**Yeniden başlatın.** Masaüstü artık monitörünüzün yenileme hızında hareket etmeli.

## 6. Denetleyin

- Uygulamanın Genel bakış sayfası sürücünün çalıştığını söyler; Bu Mac Hakkında kartın adını gösterir.
- Yardımcının son sayfası bir GPU testi çalıştırır ve ekleri sunar: Safari'yi GPU'da çalıştırma (sistem diski kopyası;
  tam kılavuz, 3.3), Minecraft Java ve diğer LWJGL oyunları için Zink üzerinden OpenGL, HiDPI modları, menü çubuğu öğesi.

## Açılmazsa

USB bellekten açın ya da OpenCore girdisi seçiliyken Shift'e basıp güvenli modda açın ve sürücüyü geri alın (paketteki
`sudo ./install.sh --undo` ya da uygulamanın Sürücü sayfası). Ayrıntılar tam kılavuzun *Açılmazsa* bölümünde; tanı
raporunun nasıl hazırlanacağı *Sorun bildirmek* bölümünde.

## Sonraki sürümler

Uygulamanın Sürücü sayfası yeni sürümü indirip eskisinin üzerine kurar; ardından EFI sayfası `IntelXe.kext`'i
değiştirir (tam kılavuz, *Yükseltme*). Bir adımın gerekip gerekmediğini sürüm notları söyler.

# Release signing keys

IntelXe Manager installs a downloaded package only when the release's list of hashes (`VERSION.sha256`) carries a
signature by one of the Ed25519 keys built into the app (`app/Sources/Signing.swift`, `releaseSigningKeys`). The
signature is `VERSION.sha256.sig` (one line, base64), made by `release/package.sh` with `SIGN_KEY=<private key file>`;
`release/release.sh` refuses to publish a release whose signature the app would not accept.

IntelXe Manager for Windows checks the same list and signature before it downloads the Xe probe stick's image
(`xe-probe-stick-VERSION.img.zip`, listed in the same `VERSION.sha256`), with its own copy of the keys:
`windows/app/IntelXe.Core/Release/ReleaseSigning.cs`, `Keys`. A key change below changes both lists in the same commit;
`ReleaseSigningTests` (`dotnet test windows/app/IntelXe.Core.Tests`) fails while they differ.

The private key never goes into a repository. Keep it in two places: the maintainer's machine (`keys/`, ignored by
git) and an offline backup (a password manager entry or an encrypted USB stick). Without it no later release can be
installed by the app; without the backup a lost disk is a lost key.

## Changing the key

A key is changed in three releases, so that every installed app keeps accepting updates. `release/release-keys.sh`
edits both apps' lists together, `package.sh` and `release.sh` check each step, and `release/test-signing.sh` runs the
whole change with throwaway keys (below).

1. **Make the new key.** `swift release/signing.swift keygen keys/intelxe-release-ed25519-2.key` prints its public key;
   back the file up as above.
2. **Release N (transition), signed by both keys.** Add the new public key to both apps (it goes after the old one, which
   stays):
   `bash release/release-keys.sh add <new public key>` (it edits `releaseSigningKeys` in `app/Sources/Signing.swift`
   and `ReleaseSigning.Keys` in `windows/app/IntelXe.Core/Release/ReleaseSigning.cs`, and refuses a malformed key, a
   key listed already, or lists that differ). Commit, build both apps from that commit, then package with both keys:
   `SIGN_KEY=keys/<old>.key SIGN_KEY_NEXT=keys/<new>.key bash release/package.sh ...`.
   That writes `VERSION.sha256.sig` (old key: what apps from before release N read) and `VERSION.sha256.sigs` (one line
   per key: what apps from release N on read). Users update the app with release N.
3. **Release N+1 and later, signed by the new key only.** `SIGN_KEY=keys/<new>.key`. Apps older than N refuse these
   releases; their users install release N first (from the release page, as a manual download) or download N+1's
   package by hand.
4. **Retire the old key.** In a later release `bash release/release-keys.sh retire <old public key>` (it never removes
   the last key); destroy the old private key and its backups once no supported app version needs it.

`bash release/release-keys.sh check` says whether the two apps list the same keys; `list` prints them.

### What the scripts check

- `package.sh`, before it writes anything: the two apps' lists are the same; `SIGN_KEY`'s public key is in them (or
  the release could not be installed by its own app); with `SIGN_KEY_NEXT`, that key is in them too and is not
  `SIGN_KEY` (the transition release must ship apps that know the key of the next one), and `SIGN_KEY_NEXT` is refused
  without `SIGN_KEY`. With `APP_DIR`, the built IntelXe Manager must carry every key of the list (its executable holds
  each as text: an app built from an older tree is refused); with `WINAPP_ZIP`, `IntelXe.Core.dll` must carry each
  (as UTF-16).
- `release.sh` (`release-keys.sh release-check`): the two apps list the same keys; `.sha256.sig` verifies with a key of
  this release's app **and** with a key of the previous release's app (`app/Sources/Signing.swift` at the last `v*`
  tag before this version: what installed apps read); every `.sha256.sigs` line verifies with a key of this release's
  app; a key this release adds must have a line in `.sha256.sigs` (without a `.sigs` file it only warns: the new key
  then signs nothing until N+1). For a lost or exposed key (below), `KEY_RESET=1` turns "the previous app cannot verify
  `.sig`" into a warning.
- The apps: the macOS app reads `.sha256.sigs` when the release has it, else `.sha256.sig` (`Model.swift`), and accepts
  any line signed by one of its keys (`releaseSignatureValid`, whose `keys` parameter the tests use); IntelXe Manager for
  Windows the same (`ProbeDownload.cs`, `ReleaseSigning.SignatureValid`). Apps up to 0.1.4 read `.sha256.sig` only,
  which is why `.sig` keeps the old key's single line during the change.

### Tests

- `bash release/test-signing.sh` (macOS, about 15 s): makes throwaway keys in a temporary folder and runs the change:
  `signing.swift` keygen/sign/verify; the app's real `Signing.swift`, compiled with a small driver, as an app before the
  change (old key, reads `.sig`), of release N (both keys, prefers `.sigs`) and after retiring (new key only), against
  releases N and N+1, one signed by another key, a changed list and a changed signature; `release-keys.sh`
  add/retire/check on copies of both lists (and an app built from the edited copy); `release-check` on each step and its
  failures; `package.sh`'s key checks. It never reads `keys/`.
- `dotnet test windows/app/IntelXe.Core.Tests --filter "FullyQualifiedName~ReleaseSigning"`: the Windows check
  (RFC 8032 vectors, a key change with two keys) and `TheKeysAreTheMacAppsKeys`, which fails while the two lists
  differ.
- The macOS app's `--selftest`: the project's key, a `.sigs` file, a key added and a key removed.

## If the private key is lost or exposed

- **Lost:** no new release can be installed by existing apps. Make a new key, `release-keys.sh add` it and `retire`
  the lost one, publish the app and packages signed by the new key (`release.sh` with `KEY_RESET=1`), and tell users
  (README, release notes) to download that app once by hand.
- **Exposed:** anyone holding it can sign a release the app accepts, if they can also publish on the release page.
  Make a new key at once, publish an app release that accepts only the new key (`release-keys.sh add` the new one,
  `retire` the exposed one; signed with the new key and checked with `KEY_RESET=1`, so users install it by hand), and
  say so in the release notes and the README. Rotate the GitHub account's credentials too.

## Checking a signature by hand

```sh
swift release/signing.swift verify <public key> intel-gpu-macos-driver-VERSION.sha256 intel-gpu-macos-driver-VERSION.sha256.sig
shasum -a 256 -c intel-gpu-macos-driver-VERSION.sha256
```

The current public key is in `app/Sources/Signing.swift` and the README.

# A desktop for a held boot: the firmware framebuffer

> Design note with its date (2026-11-13, branch `bootguard`): the plan and the state of that day. Untested on
> hardware; section 6 is the test.

## 1. The problem

The boot guard (0.1.2, IntelXeFB `guardBegin`) counts accelerated boots that end inside their first minute in NVRAM
`intelxe-guard` (`accel<n>`). From two in a row NMXAccel arms with its safest settings ("safe": no async swaps, no
flips; an accelerated login window, tested 5 Nov). From four it writes `intelxe-accel-off` and acceleration is held
on every boot until that is cleared ("held"; also `-intelxe_noaccel` and safe mode). A held boot ran IntelXeFB
alone, and on macOS 26 that stays at the Apple logo: macOS runs (SSH works) but WindowServer never draws. The only
way out without SSH was OpenCore's Reset NVRAM, and the user could not reach the IntelXe Manager to see why or to
repair.

## 2. What WindowServer needs on macOS 26 (what was measured)

From the 4-5 Nov 2026 bring-up and the held-boot tests on the B580 (project notes; nothing new was measured for this
note):

| Configuration | Result |
|---|---|
| macOS installer and first setup, no SSDT-ARCOFF, none of our kexts: Apple's IONDRVFramebuffer on the GOP's surface | desktop, unaccelerated |
| 4 Nov: IntelXeFB (class `B580IntelFramebuffer`) + NMXAGDC idle, NMXAccel not in the AuxKC, no Metal plugin installed | login window and desktop, unaccelerated |
| 5 Nov held boot (`intelxe-accel-off` set): IntelXeFB, NMXAccel registered but never armed | logo; WindowServer opened the display pipe and set the display offline |
| the same, NMXAccel not registered (test5), NMXAccel not started at all and no `IOAccelTypes` on IntelXeFB (test6) | logo |
| the same with NMXAGDC's device control brought up by hand and a WindowServer restart | logo |
| the same, then everything armed by hand (agdc, nmxaccelfb 1/3/4, iop) and WindowServer restarted | Metal compositor and `kIOWindowServerActiveAttribute` set, still the logo, 0 frame calls: a late arm is not the boot-time arm |

The held boots logged "Software compositor activated", CoreDisplay "Unable to find display pipe for IOFB service",
no "Display woke on GPU", and WindowServer never set `kIOWindowServerActiveAttribute` on IntelXeFB. So WindowServer
on 26 can run unaccelerated on a plain IOFramebuffer (the installer, and the 4 Nov boot show it), but on IntelXeFB
as it is published since the accelerated path exists (an "Intel" class name, which makes CoreDisplay take the
IOPresentment display-pipe path; the display class written back on the PCI device; `NVRMTiming`, VRR and EDID modes,
the stored display configuration of accelerated boots) it waits for a display pipe that only the boot-time arm
provides. Which of these differences decides it was not isolated: each experiment costs a held boot on the test
machine. The approach below does not depend on knowing it.

## 3. Options

1. **A minimal "dumb" IntelXeFB for held boots** (a class name without a vendor, one mode, no VRR, no cursor, no
   timing for NMXAGDC, the class code left as SSDT-ARCOFF set it). Plausible, but a guess at the unknown difference
   above, and every guess needs a held boot to check.
2. **A dumb accelerator path WindowServer accepts** (NMXAccel registered, armed with a CPU-copy pipe and no GPU
   submission). The late manual arm on 5 Nov showed WindowServer composite and still not present; the boot-time arm is
   what works, and arming at boot is exactly what the guard held because it crashed. Rejected.
3. **macOS's own fallback: the firmware framebuffer.** The path macOS takes on a GPU it has no driver for (the
   "VESA" mode of older hackintosh guides): `IONDRVFramebuffer` with its built-in `IOBootNDRV`, which publishes the
   surface the firmware lit (the boot console's framebuffer, found inside one of the device's BARs, `IOBootNDRV::
   fromRegistryEntry` in IOGraphics' IONDRVFramebuffer.cpp). It is what the macOS 26 installer ran on with this exact
   card. SSDT-ARCOFF keeps it off the card today ("#display" name, `IOName` "#display", class-code `ffffffff`), because
   it would take the IOFramebuffer match category from IntelXeFB and its controller held system sleep for 90 s.
   **Chosen.** The only new mechanism is undoing SSDT-ARCOFF's identity for one boot, which is a registry change.

There is no other unaccelerated framebuffer on macOS 26 to fall back to: OpenCore offers nothing at run time (its
GOP is gone once boot.efi exits; `-igfxvesa` is WhateverGreen's switch for Intel iGPUs, and it, too, ends in
IONDRVFramebuffer).

## 4. The design

IntelXe.kext (in the EFI, loaded before the AuxKC) decides the boot's guard state before anything is offered to
IntelXeFB:

1. **Rules in one place**: `kernel/IntelXe/uapi/intelxe_bootguard.h` (`decide`, `heldDisplay`,
   `guardAfterFirmwareHold`), plain code with no kernel calls. IntelXeFB's `guardBegin` now uses it (same behaviour;
   one deliberate change: an empty `intelxe-accel-off` counts as absent, as NMXAccel always read it). NMXAccel's
   `nmxGuardHolds` keeps its own copy (it is built separately); the host test checks the two agree.
2. **`IntelXe::bootGuardDecide`**, on the bring-up thread after IODTNVRAM is up (waited for up to 10 s, as the
   shutdown breadcrumb already was): reads `intelxe-guard`, `intelxe-accel-off`, `intelxe-held-display`, the
   boot-args `-intelxe_noaccel`, `-x` and `intelxe_helddisplay`. State: normal, retry, safe, held. A held boot shows
   the **firmware framebuffer** unless `intelxe-held-display=fb` (or `intelxe_helddisplay=1`) asks for IntelXeFB.
   Because IntelXeFB will not start, IntelXe writes what its `guardBegin` would have: the hold by count to
   `intelxe-accel-off`, and `intelxe-guard=ok` (the count is in `intelxe-accel-off` from then on, so clearing that
   alone still ends the hold, as before). Kernel writes reach flash at a clean shutdown only; after a power cut the
   old `accel4` holds the next boot the same way (tested in the host test).
3. **`IntelXe::bootGuardHandOff`**, after the bring-up loop (whether it worked or not) and before `IntelXeReady`:
   `nmxgpu-claimed` false (NMXAccel does not start), the PCI device's `name` and `IOName` back to `display`, class-code
   `03 00 00`, `IntelXeHeldDisplay` on the device, `registerService()`, `waitQuiet` up to 15 s, then it looks for the
   IOFramebuffer client. IONDRVFramebuffer (`IONameMatch display`, score 20000, category IOFramebuffer) takes the
   card. When `IntelXeReady` re-registers the device, IntelXeFB is in the same category and is not started; NMXAccel
   refuses an unclaimed GPU; NMXAGDC stays idle (it waits for an IntelXeFramebuffer). The GPU itself is still up and
   draws nothing. If IONDRVFramebuffer does not attach, `handoff=` says so and IntelXeFB starts unaccelerated, as in
   0.1.4.
4. **Visible state**: `sysctl debug.intelxe.bootguard` (and the `IntelXeBootGuard` property on IntelXe), key=value
   lines: `state`, `held_by` (count, accel-off, boot-arg, safe-mode), `reason`, `accel_fails`, `fb_fails`, `previous`,
   `held_display`, `display` (intelxefb, firmware, intelxefb-unaccelerated), `handoff`. IntelXeFB adds
   `IntelXeFBGuardState`. The IntelXe Manager's Overview page has a *Boot guard* section with the state and *Clear the
   boot guard*, which now writes `intelxe-accel-off=ok intelxe-guard=ok` (both, so a power cut in the held boot does
   not bring the hold back); the banner says when the boot runs on the firmware framebuffer. The diagnostics report
   prints the sysctl and warns `held-firmware`. The guard's LaunchDaemon (`guard-clear.sh`) stops waiting at once on
   such a boot (no IntelXeFB to clear). The macOS update guard clears both variables too.

Timing: IONDRVFramebuffer appears after the bring-up (about 15-20 s into the boot, the same moment IntelXeFB appears
on a normal boot), so WindowServer meets a late framebuffer exactly as it does today. Until then the firmware's
picture (the Apple logo) stays.

## 5. Risks and limits

- **Not run on hardware.** The registry change has to make IONDRVFramebuffer match late (a second `registerService`
  on a nub whose IOFramebuffer category is free). IOKit re-runs matching for unmatched categories on
  `registerService`; IntelXe already relies on that for IntelXeFB and NMXAccel. IONameMatch on an IOPCIDevice
  compares the `name` property (`IODTCompareNubName`), which is what is restored.
- **WindowServer might still not draw on IONDRVFramebuffer** with our other parts installed (the Metal plugin on the
  system volume, NMXAGDC loaded, the display configuration saved by accelerated boots). The installer had none of
  them. If so, section 6 step 7 collects what is needed; the way out stays Reset NVRAM, as today.
- **Sleep**: SSDT-ARCOFF exists partly because IONDRVFramebuffer's controller held system sleep for 90 s on this card.
  A held boot is for repairing; the Manager says not to sleep it. On a wake IntelXe clears VRAM below 32 MB (the
  firmware's surface) as it does today.
- **One resolution** (the GOP's), no acceleration, no Metal, no HiDPI, no Adaptive-Sync, no hot-plug.
- The renamed device (`display`) is offered to every driver once more; in the installer nothing but
  IONDRVFramebuffer took it.
- A panic inside the hand-off would repeat on every held boot: Reset NVRAM clears the hold (normal boots never run
  the hand-off), or `intelxe-held-display=fb`, or the USB stick's EFI.
- Safe mode: IntelXe.kext is `OSBundleRequired Root`; if it loads in safe mode, safe mode now gets the firmware
  framebuffer too (before, nothing drove the display). Not checked.

## 6. Hardware test (B580, by hand; nothing runs by itself)

Before: Remote Login on; a second machine with SSH; the USB stick keeps the proven EFI (F8); OpenCore's picker shows
Reset NVRAM (Space). Each remote command is short (under a minute). Build: `build.py --release` for both kexts;
IntelXe.kext into the SN550 EFI (`efi.sh` / the EFI page), IntelXeFB.kext with `install.sh --apply` (the AuxKC is
rebuilt), restart. Keep `TALLogoutSavesState`/`LoginwindowLaunchesRelaunchApps` false before each restart.

1. **Normal boot.** `sysctl debug.intelxe.bootguard`: `state=normal`, `display=intelxefb`, `handoff=not needed`.
   Accelerated desktop as before; the Manager's Overview shows *Boot guard: Normal*.
2. **Held by `intelxe-accel-off`.** `sudo nvram intelxe-accel-off=test`, restart. Expect the Apple logo for about
   20 s, then the login window on the firmware framebuffer (no transparency, 2560x1440 at the GOP's rate). Over SSH:
   `sysctl debug.intelxe.bootguard` (`state=held`, `held_by=accel-off`, `display=firmware`,
   `handoff=IONDRVFramebuffer attached`); `ioreg -rc IONDRVFramebuffer -d1 | head -20`;
   `ioreg -rc IntelXeFramebuffer -d1 | head -3` (nothing); `kmutil showloaded --list-only | grep -i -e nmx -e intelxe`;
   `log show --last boot --style compact --predicate 'eventMessage CONTAINS "boot guard"' | tail -5`. Log in; the
   Manager shows *Acceleration held* with the reason `test`. Do not sleep the machine.
3. **Clear from that desktop.** The Manager's *Clear the boot guard* (password), then restart. Expect a normal
   accelerated boot; `nvram intelxe-accel-off intelxe-guard` both `ok`.
4. **Held by the count.** `sudo nvram intelxe-guard=accel4`, restart. Expect step 2's desktop with `held_by=count`;
   `nvram intelxe-guard` reads `ok` and `intelxe-accel-off` reads "4 accelerated boots in a row ended inside their
   first minute" (the kernel's writes). Restart once more without clearing: still held, now `held_by=accel-off`.
   Clear over SSH with `sudo nvram intelxe-accel-off=ok intelxe-guard=ok`, restart: normal.
5. **Safe state shown.** `sudo nvram intelxe-guard=accel2`, restart: accelerated login window (as on 5 Nov),
   `state=safe`, the Manager shows *Safe settings*; after a minute on the desktop `nvram intelxe-guard` is `ok`.
6. **The old behaviour on request (optional).** `sudo nvram intelxe-accel-off=test intelxe-held-display=fb`,
   restart: the logo stays (0.1.4's held boot), `display=intelxefb-unaccelerated`. Undo over SSH:
   `sudo nvram intelxe-accel-off=ok intelxe-held-display=ok`, restart.
7. **If step 2 stays at the logo**: it is not a hang; over SSH collect `sysctl debug.intelxe.bootguard`,
   `ioreg -rc IOFramebuffer -d1 | grep -E 'class|IOFBDependent' | head`,
   `ioreg -l -w0 | grep -E '"(name|IOName|class-code)" = .*(display|0300)' | head`,
   `log show --last boot --style compact --predicate 'process == "WindowServer"' | grep -iE 'display|framebuffer|compositor' | tail -40`,
   then `sudo nvram intelxe-accel-off=ok intelxe-guard=ok && sudo reboot`. Without SSH: Reset NVRAM in the picker.
   A panic loop: Reset NVRAM (clears the hold), or F8 and the USB stick's EFI.

Recovery in every case: `sudo nvram intelxe-accel-off=ok intelxe-guard=ok intelxe-held-display=ok` and restart, or
Reset NVRAM, or the USB stick.

## 7. Files and tests

`kernel/IntelXe/uapi/intelxe_bootguard.h` (rules), `kernel/IntelXe/IntelXe.cpp` (`bootGuardDecide`,
`bootGuardHandOff`, `debug.intelxe.bootguard`), `kernel/IntelXeFB/IntelXeFB.cpp` (`guardBegin` on the shared rules,
`IntelXeFBGuardState`), `release/templates/install.sh` (`guard-clear.sh`), `app/Sources/Model.swift`
(`BootGuardStatus`), `Views.swift` (*Boot guard* section, the clear), `Health.swift`, `SelfTest.swift`,
`app/Resources/osupdate-guard.sh`, `tools/report/collect-macos.sh`.

- `kernel/IntelXe/tests/bootguard_test.cpp` (550 checks): parsing; `decide` against IntelXeFB's 0.1.4 rules and
  NMXAccel's over every combination of guard value, `intelxe-accel-off` and the two boot-args; the held display
  setting; several boots in a row (crashes to safe and held, the held boot's writes, clearing from its desktop, a
  power cut that loses them, the old one-variable clear). A mutation of the hold count or of the guard clear fails it.
- `IntelXeManager --selftest` (the status parser and texts; the `system-held` snapshot),
  `app/tests/test-osupdate-guard.sh` (both variables cleared), `release/test-install-flow.sh` (the daemon script
  parses).
- Kext builds: no new warnings (22 IntelXe, 24 IntelXeFB).

# Direct submission in IntelXe.kext (design, 2026-11-09)

> Design note with its date: it records the plan and the state of that day, not the current status.
>
> Update (2026-11-10): merged and released in 0.1.4, still off by default (`debug.intelxe.direct=1` until the next
> restart); one armed queue at a time. Measured on the B580: a tiny job's exec -> signal 46-52 -> 15-17 us, Geekbench 7
> Metal 97.2k, OpenCL 92.9k. Current state: the README, `docs/ROADMAP.md` and `docs/devices/b580.md`.
>
> Update (2026-11-12): after an unattended night (idle, sleep and wake, repeated Geekbench runs: no fault) and a power
> check (no idle cost; +7 W card power while a stream of tiny jobs keeps a queue armed, open item 1 below), on by default
> in the tree (`-intelxe_nodirect`: off). Numbers: `docs/ROADMAP.md`, "Submission cost and latency".

## Why

One tiny Metal command buffer (one dispatch) takes 56 us from commit to the waiter waking at 2850 MHz, 94 us at the
1200 MHz SLPC floor; Windows takes 5.4 us (`user/tests/metal/mtl_lat.m split`). The job-timing kext
(`debug.intelxe.jobtime`, RING_TIMESTAMP stores in the ring) splits the 56 us:

| step | us (2850 MHz) |
|---|---|
| exec ioctl entry to H2G SCHED_CONTEXT | 2.7 |
| H2G to the ring starting the job (GuC scheduling, context load) | **29** |
| pre-batch invalidate | 1.5 |
| the batch | 8.6 |
| end-of-job flush and seqno store | 0.8 |
| to the interrupt | ~7 |
| interrupt to the waiter running | 3 |

The largest step is the GuC putting the context on the engine for every job. `user/tests/kernel/ulls.c` (4e7a52b)
showed that a context which stays on the engine, polling a mailbox with `MI_SEMAPHORE_WAIT`, starts a job 4.0-4.6 us
after the CPU's write, against 28.5-34.7 us through the exec path. That is Intel's "ULLS" (ultra-low-latency
submission) of the compute runtime, done there in user space.

## Where: the kernel, not Mesa or the plugin

User-space ULLS (the compute runtime's way) bypasses the kernel's fences: every syncobj, IOSurface mark, the
WindowServer handoff and the job watchdog would have to learn about jobs the kernel never saw. In the kext, nothing
above it changes: `DRM_IOCTL_XE_EXEC` stays the submission call (2.7 us), seqnos, fences, syncobjs, bans and GT-reset
replay keep working, and only the path from the ioctl to the engine gets shorter. Mesa and the Metal plugin stay
as they are.

## How: the ring keeps one slot armed

Today `queueEmitEx` writes a job's dwords into the context's ring (GGTT), sets the LRC tail and sends
SCHED_CONTEXT (0x1000). In direct mode a queue's ring always ends with one **armed slot** for the next seqno `s`:

```
[MI_SEMAPHORE_WAIT  poll, GGTT mailbox >= s]          // the context stays on the engine here
[pre-job PIPE_CONTROL invalidate]                       // fixed (jobDwords' first part)
[MI_BATCH_BUFFER_START first level, GGTT -> stub[s % N]]
[end-of-job flush, seqno s store, MI_USER_INTERRUPT, MI_ARB_CHECK]   // fixed: s is known in advance
```

and the LRC tail ends right after it. The stub (a few dwords in kernel GGTT memory, one per slot) is written at
submit time: an optional TLB-invalidating PIPE_CONTROL when the VM's page tables changed, then a chained
`MI_BATCH_BUFFER_START` (first level, PPGTT) to the application's batch, whose `MI_BATCH_BUFFER_END` returns to the
ring. Prefetch is safe: the ring dwords are all written before the slot is armed, and the stub is only read after
the jump that follows the semaphore.

Submitting job `s` in direct mode: write the stub, `deviceWmb`, write `s` to the mailbox (the latency path ends
here), then append the armed slot for `s + 1` and move the tail with SCHED_CONTEXT. That H2G is off the latency
path: the context is already running, so the GuC only updates its tail.

**Leaving direct mode** (no job for `debug.intelxe.direct_idle_us`, default about 2 ms; another queue submitting to
the same engine class; suspend; a GT reset): the kext submits a no-op job into the armed slot (stub = a bare
`MI_BATCH_BUFFER_END`, seqno consumed like an empty kernel job) **without** arming another slot. The ring runs dry,
the context goes idle and the GuC switches it out, so the engine can reach RC6 and other contexts run without
timeslicing against a polling one. The next job takes the normal path (SCHED_CONTEXT) and re-arms.

**Entering direct mode**: a queue with the low-latency hint (`DRM_XE_EXEC_QUEUE_LOW_LATENCY_HINT`, which the plugin
already sets for applications and never for WindowServer and the system UI) on the compute class whose jobs arrive
less than about the idle limit apart. Render stays on the normal path: WindowServer shares the render engine and
would be timesliced against a polling context.

*Changed after the first measurements (9 Nov, evening):* the GuC low-latency hint became opt-in (a GPU fault after
long idle), and Geekbench's OpenCL and Metal work turned out to run on the render class (its faults named class 0).
Now any application queue of the render or compute class may arm, the hint no longer matters, and the kext keeps
WindowServer and the system's interface out by process name. On the render class WindowServer's next frame is
"another queue on the armed one's class": the armed queue leaves before that frame goes to the ring. Measured with
the compute class first: a 180 fps animation stayed at 179 fps with direct mode on or off under load.

## What stays the same

- Fences: the seqno store and user interrupt are in the ring as now; `done` and `submitted` mean what they mean now.
  A queue waiting at an armed slot has `done == submitted`, so the watchdog sees it as idle and times only real jobs.
- Faults and bans: a CAT error or context reset still arrives per guc_id, so the queue is banned as now; the armed
  slot goes with the ring.
- GT reset: replay rewinds the ring head to the first unfinished job as now; the armed slot is just ring contents.
  The mailbox is reset to the replayed seqno.
- Suspend: leave direct mode first, as `xeSuspend` already drains the queues.
- Long-running VMs (branch `lrmode`, DESIGN-lr-mode.md section 3): an LR queue arms and leaves under the same rules; the
  LR preemption (a BO move, a deferred free's cycle) makes an armed queue leave before it closes the ring ("other").

## Risks and checks before code

1. A context polling `MI_SEMAPHORE_WAIT` keeps SLPC busy and the GT out of RC6 while armed. Measure the power with
   the idle limit at 0.5, 2 and 10 ms (`step=20` energy counter) against the latency it buys.
2. GuC timeslicing against a polling context: with two direct-mode queues on the CCS, the second must not wait up to
   one timeslice. The "another queue submits, leave direct mode" rule covers it; test with two `ulls`.
3. The jump to a GGTT stub from the ring and the chained jump from the stub to a PPGTT batch: verify on the hardware
   (kext build behind `debug.intelxe.direct`, off by default).
4. SCHED_CONTEXT for a context that is running a job: confirm (job timing) that the GuC moves the tail without
   preempting or stalling the job.
5. The `ulls chain` mode (a second-level batch that chains, as an ANV batch would if called at the second level)
   tells whether the alternative layout (stub called at the second level, post-job commands in a persistent batch)
   is available.

## Expected gain

The 29 us of GuC scheduling becomes about 4 us. A tiny command buffer would go from about 56 to 31 us at 2850 MHz
and from 94 to about 55 us at 1200 MHz. Windows is still ahead in the batch (8.6 us), the interrupt path (10 us)
and the plugin's CPU cost per command buffer (back to back 18-21 us against 1.9: the plugin's class-wide lock),
which is separate work.

## Implementation (branch direct-submit, 2026-11-09, untested on the hardware)

`xe_core.cpp`, section "direct submission"; `debug.intelxe.direct` (default 0) and `debug.intelxe.direct_idle_us`
(default 2000); counters in the "direct submission" line of `debug.intelxe.stats`. Differences from the plan above:

- The whole pre-job part (preparser off, the invalidating PIPE_CONTROL, preparser on, CTX_TIMESTAMP and start seqno)
  is in the stub, not in the ring: the TLB-invalidate bit depends on the job, and one PIPE_CONTROL is cheaper than two.
  The ring slot is preparser off, `MI_SEMAPHORE_WAIT`, preparser on (as the compute runtime disables the prefetcher
  around its semaphore), the jump to the stub, and `jobPost`.
- Back-to-back jobs: each submit arms the slot for the next seqno before it returns, so a job submitted while the
  previous one runs finds its slot armed; there is no fallback to the normal path for it.
- Entering: a job on the normal path arms the next slot when the queue's previous job was less than the idle limit ago
  and no other queue used the compute class in that time; so the first two jobs of a burst take the normal path.
- An exec that has to wait in the FIFO (in-fences, a held queue) makes the queue leave first: an armed queue's FIFO is
  always empty, so the no-op never takes a seqno a fence already has.
- A GT reset makes the queue leave before the reset; the replay then passes every slot left in the ring, since the
  mailbox only grows within a stretch, and a new stretch starts only once the last one's slots have all run.
- Stubs: 256 per queue (one per `ringPos` entry; job x's stub is written only after job x - 256 completed), 32 entries
  of 32 KB plus a mailbox page in system memory, GGTT-mapped at the first `debug.intelxe.direct=1`.
- rb8e (12 Nov, untested on the B580): exec user fences. Until then a job carrying `DRM_XE_SYNC_TYPE_USER_FENCE` made
  the armed queue leave (the slot's `jobPost` is written at arming time and had no store for it), so with ANV's
  `ANV_UFENCE=1` (a user fence on every exec with a batch) no queue stayed armed. Now the slot's `jobPost` calls a
  per-seqno **post-stub** (first-level `MI_BATCH_BUFFER_START`, GGTT) between the end-of-job flush and the seqno store,
  where the ring path stores the user fence: it holds `MI_STORE_DATA_IMM | MI_SDI_NUM_QW(1)` to the fence's PPGTT
  address (render/compute; copy/video would get `MI_FLUSH_DW` first, as `xe_ring_ops.c`) and `MI_BATCH_BUFFER_END`, or
  the return alone (`xe_direct.h xeDsPostStub`). It is written with the stub before the mailbox and follows the stubs'
  reuse rule (256 per queue, 64 bytes each, after the stubs in the same GGTT-mapped memory). Counted:
  `debug.intelxe.stats` "submits N (with a user fence M)".
- tlbinring (13 Nov, branch `tlbinring`, untested on the B580, `debug.intelxe.tlb_inring`, default 0): an exec whose
  pending in-fences are all TLB invalidations (a VM_BIND out-fence since rb8d, which Mesa's bind timeline hands every
  exec after an unbind) made the armed queue leave like any other in-fence, so OpenCL's map/unmap per operation kept
  taking queues out of direct submission (DESIGN-rb8-cost.md, findings 1-2). With the knob at 1 such a job goes into
  the armed slot anyway and its **stub starts with `MI_SEMAPHORE_WAIT` on the TLB word** (a GGTT dword at page 0 + 0x800
  of the stub memory, after the mailboxes, which the CPU sets to the invalidation done seqno from the G2H handler,
  `xeTlbWordPublish`), inside the preparser-disabled part before the invalidating `PIPE_CONTROL`: the batch, its user
  fence and seqno run only once the invalidations completed, as Linux's drm_sched dependency orders them. The queue
  stays armed. A stub is then at most 32 dwords (job timing and a batch): exactly `kDsStubBytes`. Knob 2 does the same
  on the normal ring path. Safety argument, Linux references, counters: DESIGN-rb8-cost.md "tlbinring".

# Display boost: the GT clock while frames miss their vblank

> Design note with its date (2026-11-14, branch `dispboost`): it records the plan and the state of that day, not the
> current status. Default on while it is measured on the B580; the measurement decides the default.

## 1. The problem (B580, macOS 26, 180 Hz, HiDPI 4096x2304 backing, 14 Nov)

`user/tests/wsi/p4check.m smooth -v` (a 640x360 pt CAMetalLayer window, displaySync on, 3 drawables, one clear per
frame): in steady state 0 of ~1790 frames late in 10 s. Started after the GPU was idle, the first ~370 ms run at 90 Hz
(every frame two refreshes, ~20-23 late frames, the app's `nextDrawable` blocks ~8 ms), then 180 Hz. With
`sysctl debug.intelxe.slpc_min=2850` the same start has 0-1 late frames. So what is left is the SLPC ramp from idle (floor
1200 MHz, RP0 2850): WindowServer's composite at this size is ~1.37 ms per command buffer and ~3.6 command buffers per
frame, which at the idle clock does not fit in 5.56 ms. SLPC raises the clock from its own busyness samples, which
take a few hundred ms to see a desktop that has just started animating.

## 2. What Linux does (read in torvalds/linux v7.4-rc2, commit 7475ea8b5861, 8 Nov 2026)

### i915: a boost when a flip misses its vblank

- `drivers/gpu/drm/i915/display/intel_plane.c` `intel_prepare_plane_fb()`: for a plane state with a fence,
  `intel_display_rps_boost_after_vblank(crtc, fence)`, then `intel_display_rps_mark_interactive(..., true)`.
- `drivers/gpu/drm/i915/display/intel_display_rps.c` `intel_display_rps_boost_after_vblank()`: if the parent driver has an
  rps interface (`intel_parent_rps_available()`), takes a vblank reference and adds a wait entry to the crtc's vblank wait
  queue. At the next vblank `do_rps_boost()` calls `intel_parent_rps_boost_if_not_started(display, fence)` once and frees
  the entry. Its comment: "If we missed the vblank, but the request is already running it is reasonable to assume that
  it will complete before the next vblank without our intervention, so leave RPS alone if not started."
- `drivers/gpu/drm/i915/gt/intel_rps.c` `boost_if_not_started()` (the `i915_display_rps_interface`): an i915 fence whose
  request has not started (`!i915_request_started(rq)`) gets `intel_rps_boost(rq)`.
- `intel_rps_boost()` (same file): nothing for a signalled or already boosted request, nothing for a context with
  `CONTEXT_LOW_LATENCY`; sets `I915_FENCE_FLAG_BOOST`; with GuC SLPC nothing under the power-saving profile
  (`SLPC_POWER_PROFILES_POWER_SAVING`), else `atomic_fetch_inc(&slpc->num_waiters)` and, on the first waiter, unless
  `min_freq_softlimit >= boost_freq`, queues `slpc->boost_work`.
- `drivers/gpu/drm/i915/gt/uc/intel_guc_slpc.c` `slpc_boost_work()` -> `slpc_force_min_freq(slpc, slpc->boost_freq)`: a
  non-blocking `SLPC_PARAM_GLOBAL_MIN_GT_UNSLICE_FREQ_MHZ` that leaves the user's soft limit alone. `boost_freq` is RP0
  unless set (`slpc_get_rp_values`; sysfs `gt_boost_freq_mhz`, `intel_guc_slpc_set_boost_freq`).
- It ends with the request: `drivers/gpu/drm/i915/i915_request.c` `i915_request_retire()` -> `intel_rps_dec_waiters()` ->
  `intel_guc_slpc_dec_waiters()`: when `num_waiters` drops to 0, `slpc_force_min_freq(slpc, min_freq_softlimit)`. No
  timer: the floor stays up exactly while some boosted request is unfinished.
- `intel_rps_mark_interactive()` only changes host RPS thresholds; with SLPC `intel_rps_enable()` returns before
  `intel_rps_set_active()`, so it does nothing.

### i915: waitboost

- `i915_request.c` `i915_request_wait_timeout()`: `if (flags & I915_WAIT_PRIORITY && !i915_request_started(rq))
  intel_rps_boost(rq)` before sleeping. `I915_WAIT_PRIORITY` comes from `i915_fence_wait()` (the dma_fence `.wait`, so any
  `dma_fence_wait()` on an i915 fence), `gem/i915_gem_wait.c` (GEM_WAIT; it first boosts every not-started fence of the
  reservation, `i915_gem_object_boost`) and `gem/i915_gem_domain.c` (set-domain).
- `drivers/gpu/drm/drm_syncobj.c` `drm_syncobj_array_wait_timeout()` does not call the fence's `.wait`: it adds callbacks
  and sleeps, and calls `dma_fence_set_deadline()` only when the caller passes `DRM_SYNCOBJ_WAIT_FLAGS_WAIT_DEADLINE`.
  Neither i915 nor xe implements `.set_deadline`. So a Vulkan driver's fence waits (syncobjs) never waitboost, on i915
  either. (msm does use deadlines: `drivers/gpu/drm/msm/msm_fence.c` `deadline_work()` -> `msm_devfreq_boost()`, with
  `drm_atomic_helper.c` `set_fence_deadline()` giving plane fences the next vblank start.)

### xe: nothing of the kind

- `drivers/gpu/drm/xe`: no occurrence of "boost" at all.
- The display code is the same (`xe/Makefile` builds `i915-display/intel_display_rps.o`), but `xe/display/xe_display.c`'s
  `intel_display_parent_interface` has no `.rps`, so `intel_parent_rps_available()` is false and
  `intel_display_rps_boost_after_vblank()` returns at once.
- xe leaves the clock to SLPC: `xe_guc_pc.c` sets `SLPC_OPTIMIZED_STRATEGY_COMPUTE` and the power profile (sysfs
  `power_profile`, `xe_gt_freq.c`), and a queue created with `DRM_XE_EXEC_QUEUE_LOW_LATENCY_HINT` gets
  `SLPC_CTX_FREQ_REQ_IS_COMPUTE` in its GuC policy (`xe_exec_queue.c`, `xe_guc_submit.c`).

## 3. What this stack has

- The present path (stage 2/3 of `framepath.md`, phase 4): WindowServer does not wait for its composite. The Metal
  plugin marks the composite surface pending at commit and ready when its GPU work is done; NMXAccel's present worker
  (`nullmoth/kexts/NVRM/accel/nvrm-accel.cpp` `nmxPresent`) waits for the mark (`nvSurfWaitReady`), then flips (or
  copies). That wait is the one place the kernel knows "this frame is presented, its GPU work is not done": the
  equivalent of i915's plane fence at `prepare_fb`.
- The vblank: IntelXeFB times it (`vblFire`, `usSinceVblank()`: `TIMESTAMP_CTR - PIPE_FRMTMSTMP`, microseconds) and
  publishes the frame length (`NVRMFlipWaitUs`, 5/4 of a frame).
- The clock: `xe_slpcboost.h`'s lease on SLPC's minimum (slpc_boost, 13 Nov), with its timer, the sleep handling and
  the rule that the minimum the GuC gets is the highest of the administrator's floor and the leases, clamped to
  `slpc_max`.
- CPU waits on GPU fences: `xe_core.cpp` `syncobjWait` (SYNCOBJ_WAIT / TIMELINE_WAIT) and `waitUserFence`.

## 4. The choice

(a) display boost: implemented. (b) waitboost: not implemented, because:

- Linux xe has none, and i915 has none on the path a Vulkan driver uses (syncobj waits, section 2);
- here every WindowServer composite is waited for by the plugin's worker (`vkWaitForFences`), so a waitboost without
  i915's "not started" test would fire on every desktop frame, video included; the kernel has no cheap "has this job
  started" per fence;
- the measurement points at the display: the late frames are composites; (a) sees them directly.

## 5. Design

**Trigger (NMXAccel, `nmx_vbldue.h`, `nmxPresent`).** When the present worker takes a frame whose surface is still
pending, it works out when the frame was due: the first start of vblank after `t0`, the time the worker took it (its
present, or, for a frame that waited behind another, the landing of that one). The phase comes from IntelXeFB's
`nmxScanout` op 4 (NMXScanout version 4: `vblAgoNs` since the last start of vblank, `frameNs`); without it (an older
IntelXeFB, the second pipe) one frame after `t0` (any interval of one frame holds a start of vblank). The wait
(`nvSurfWaitReadyDue`) sleeps until the due time; a frame still pending then missed its vblank: NMXAccel counts it
(`debug.nmxaccel_vbl_miss`) and calls IntelXe's `intelxeDispBoost` once, then waits on as before. Like i915, the boost is
asked at the vblank, while the late frame is still running. Unlike i915 there is no "not started" test (no cheap
per-frame started bit for a plugin mark): "not done at the vblank" is the condition.

**Lease (IntelXe, `xe_slpcboost.h` `XeDispLease`, `xe_core.cpp` `dispRun`).** `intelxeDispBoost` never blocks: it counts
the miss and enters a thread call that takes `gDevLock` and applies the rules:

- a miss while a display lease runs renews it: it ends `disp_boost_ms` (50 ms) after the last miss;
- without a lease, misses less than a lease length apart form a streak; the `disp_boost_misses`-th (2) starts a lease,
  so one late frame of an idle desktop does not lift the clock (`1` = i915's every miss);
- at most 5 new leases a second (renewals send nothing and are not counted);
- the floor is `disp_boost_mhz`, 0 = the ceiling (RP0, i915's `boost_freq`), always clamped to [RPn, `slpc_max`]; the
  GuC gets the highest of `slpc_min`, a `slpc_boost` lease and the display lease, sent as slpc_boost sends it
  (`IGNORE_EFFICIENT_FREQUENCY` + `GLOBAL_MIN_GT_UNSLICE_FREQ_MHZ`); the lease's end arms the slpc_boost timer, which
  sends the floor back;
- nothing while switched off, while `debug.intelxe.freq_manual` is set, with the power-saving SLPC profile
  (`slpc_profile 1`, as i915's `intel_rps_boost`) or while the GT cannot take a new minimum (reset, sleep, no SLPC);
  each is counted;
- system sleep ends the lease (`xeBoostSleep`), and so does writing 0 to `disp_boost` (the floor goes back at once).

Why a lease and not i915's "until the request retires": the late frame's work is done in a few ms, and SLPC's own
estimate needs longer than that to follow; a 50 ms lease renewed by each miss holds the clock while frames keep missing
and lets go 50 ms after the last one. The cost is bounded by the misses: a desktop whose frames are on time never boosts.

**Knobs and counters.**

| Name | What |
|---|---|
| `debug.intelxe.disp_boost` | 1 on (default), 0 off (ends a running lease); root writes |
| boot-arg `-intelxe_nodispboost` | 0 from the start |
| `debug.intelxe.disp_boost_ms` | lease length, 10-200 ms (200 since the B580 results below; was 50) |
| `debug.intelxe.disp_boost_misses` | streak that starts a lease, 1-8 (1; was 2) |
| `debug.intelxe.disp_boost_mhz` | floor, 0 = RP0 / `slpc_max` (0) |
| `debug.intelxe.disp_boost_stats` | anyone: `disp_boost lease_ms misses_needed floor_mhz active left_ms misses grants renewals streak ratelimited off manual powersave notready expiries sleepends switchoffs boosted_ms` (name value pairs; also in `debug.intelxe.dump` as `[disp_boost]`) |
| `debug.nmxaccel_vbl_miss` | frames still on the GPU at the vblank they were due at (counted with the boost off too) |
| `debug.nmxaccel_vbl_due` / `_nophase` / `_unknown` | presents of a pending frame, due from IntelXeFB's phase / one refresh after t0 / not checked |
| `debug.nmxaccel_vbl_boost_fail` | misses IntelXe did not take (an older IntelXe.kext) |

## 6. Measuring it (`user/tests/wsi/night-dispboost.sh`)

For boost off and on, five times each, interleaved (ABBA): wait until the GT is idle (`debug.intelxe.sensors` act at or
below the idle clock for 3 s), run `p4check smooth -t 3 -v` with the GT clock sampled every 25 ms, and record the late
frames in the first 500 ms and overall, the clock ramp, `debug.nmxaccel_vbl_miss` and the boost counters. Then 20 s of
idle desktop with each setting (and 20 s of video if a player is given): misses, leases, time boosted, mean clock and
the card's average power from the PMT energy counter. What decides the default: late frames in the first 500 ms with
the boost on near the `slpc_min=2850` result (0-1), and at idle / video few leases and a power difference within the
noise.

## 7. Files

- `kernel/IntelXe/xe_slpcboost.h`: `XeDispLease`, `xeDispMiss`, `xeDispEnd`, `xeDispSwitchOff`, and the display lease in
  `xeBoostEffectiveMin` / `xeBoostExpire` / `xeBoostSleep` / `xeBoostNextNs`.
- `kernel/IntelXe/xe_core.cpp`: `dispRun`, `xeDispBoostMiss`, `xeDispBoostSet`, `xeDispBoostStats`, `gDispCall`.
- `kernel/IntelXe/IntelXe.cpp`: the sysctls, the boot-arg, the dump section; `IntelXeClient.cpp`: `intelxeDispBoost`.
- `kernel/IntelXeFB/IntelXeFB.cpp`: NMXScanout version 4 (op 4 answers the vblank phase).
- `nullmoth/kexts/NVRM/accel/nmx_vbldue.h`, `nvrm-accel.cpp` (`nmxVblDueAbs`, `nmxVblMissed`, `nvSurfWaitReadyDue`).
- Tests: `kernel/IntelXe/tests/dispboost_test.cpp`, `nullmoth/kexts/NVRM/accel/tests/nmx_vbldue_test.cpp`.

## B580 results and the idle-exit trigger (14 Nov 2026)

First run with the defaults above (2 misses within 50 ms, 50 ms lease): no change (about 23 late frames per start from
idle, boost off or on). NMXAccel saw only ~3 misses per start: in the ~370 ms SLPC ramp WindowServer composites every
other refresh, but its frames are rarely still on the GPU at the vblank they were due at, so the miss trigger fires
seldom and late. Measured instead:

| Setting (8 starts from idle each, `p4check smooth -t 3 -v`) | late frames (sum) | per start | fps |
|---|---|---|---|
| boost off | 206 | 23-42 | 170.8 |
| boost on: 1 miss starts a 200 ms lease, plus the idle-exit trigger | 16 | 0-5 | 179.0 |

Reference: `slpc_min` pinned at 2400 MHz gives 1-25 late per start; 2000 MHz gives 4-5.

**Idle-exit trigger** (NMXAccel, `debug.nmxaccel_idle_boost_ms`, default 250, 0 = off; counter
`debug.nmxaccel_idle_boosts`): the first frame after the display was quiet that long asks IntelXe for the boost at once,
so the clock is raised when the ramp starts, not after frames have already been missed. Defaults changed to
`disp_boost_misses` 1 and `disp_boost_ms` 200.

Cost: idle desktop 20 s, 36.58 W off / 36.57 W on, no leases. Periodic small updates (a window changing colour every
600 ms, like a blinking caret): a lease on every update (31% of the time boosted), card power 36.70 / 37.96 W off,
36.66 / 36.65 W on, so no measurable cost. Video playback was not sampled (QuickTime automation was refused); it
presents without quiet gaps, so only the miss trigger can fire there.

## Final defaults (14 Nov 2026, evening): the idle-exit lease alone

Video cost of the miss trigger (AVPlayer looping a clip in a 1280x720 window, 20 s, card power from PMT): H.264 4K60
55.4 W off / 63.4 W on (lease 54% of the time), HEVC10 4K60 50.7 W / 61.0 W (lease 100% of the time, misses ~58 a second
whether boosted or not: boosting did not reduce them). 1080p30: no change. So the idle-exit trigger now has its own
entry ("intelxeDispBoostIdle" -> xeDispBoostIdle, a lease of `debug.intelxe.disp_boost_idle_ms`, default 400, at once,
not through the miss streak), and `debug.intelxe.disp_boost_misses` 0 switches the miss trigger off: that is the default.

12 starts from idle each (`p4check smooth -t 2 -v`, two interleaved rounds):

| Setting | late frames (sum) | worst start | fps |
|---|---|---|---|
| boost off | 303 | 44 | 166.8 |
| idle exit only, 200 ms | 88 | 43 | 176.1 |
| **idle exit only, 400 ms (default)** | **13** | **2** | **179.3** |
| idle exit 400 ms + miss trigger | 14 | 3 | 179.1 |

Video with the default: H.264 4K60 56.0 W, HEVC10 4K60 51.6 W, no lease taken (a playing video never leaves the display
quiet for 250 ms). The miss trigger stays available (`disp_boost_misses` 1-8) for experiments.

# Vulkan fd sharing on macOS without real dma-buf/sync_file fds (design, 2026-10-30)

> Design note with its date: it records the plan and the state of that day, not the current status. The current
> state is in the README and `docs/devices/b580.md`.

Goal: `VK_KHR_external_memory_fd` (+ `VK_EXT_external_memory_dma_buf`), `VK_KHR_external_semaphore_fd` and
`VK_KHR_external_fence_fd` on ANV over IntelXe.kext, **across processes**: Wine's shared resources (D3D11/12 shared
handles, the DXGI swapchain between the game and the compositor process) map `*_win32` handles onto the host's fd
extensions, and wineserver hands the fds from process to process with `SCM_RIGHTS`. Today xemac answers
`PRIME_*` and `SYNCOBJ_*_FD` with ENOTTY.

XeGfx's answer (HOW.md "Fences without file descriptors") makes the stand-ins in userspace (the read end of a pipe,
told apart by inode) and keeps the kernel side per DRM file, so it cannot share between processes, cannot `poll()`
a sync_file and cannot merge. Wine needs the cross-process part, so the kernel has to recognise the stand-in itself.

## 1. The stand-in: an unlinked file the kernel can identify

A kext cannot make file descriptors, but it can look at one the caller passes in. With public KPIs only
(com.apple.kpi.bsd: `file_vnode_withvid`, `file_drop`, `vnode_vid`, `vnode_getwithvid`, `vnode_isinuse`,
`vnode_put`) the stand-in is a regular file nobody can reach by name:

- Export (xemac): `mkstemp()` in the process's temporary directory (sandboxed processes have their own), `unlink()` at
  once, `ftruncate()` to the BO size (sparse: no disk space; `lseek(fd, 0, SEEK_END)`, which Mesa and libdrm use to
  read a dma-buf's size, then just works), and the fd passed in the export ioctl. The kext resolves it
  (`file_vnode_withvid` -> vnode + vid) and records **(vnode pointer, vid)** as the key of a new export entry.
- Import (any process; the fd came by dup, fork or `SCM_RIGHTS`, it is the same open file): the kext resolves the fd
  and compares (vnode, vid). Not found -> EINVAL, as Linux answers an fd that is not a dma-buf. The pair cannot be
  forged or guessed: only a holder of the fd can present that vnode, and a vnode recycled for another file has a new
  vid, so a stale pointer never matches.
- Lifetime, as a dma-buf (alive while an fd or an import holds it): the entry must go when the last fd is closed. An
  unlinked file's vnode is inactivated and reclaimed on its last close (its vid changes). The kext checks its entries
  on every export/import and from a timer (every few seconds while entries exist): `vnode_getwithvid(vp, vid)` fails
  (recycled) or `vnode_isinuse(vp, 0)` is false (no open file left) -> the entry and its BO reference go.
- Not possible this way (and not needed by Vulkan or Wine, which wait through vkWait*/syncobjs): `poll()` waiting for
  a sync_file to signal (a regular file always polls readable). XeGfx cannot either.

Rejected: an AF_UNIX socketpair (`file_socket` is public, but keeping the kext's end alive and being told of the
peer's close needs `sock_retain` / `sock_setupcall`, which are KERNEL_PRIVATE); a pipe (no KPI resolves a pipe fd);
mach ports or IOSurface-style global ids (Wine moves fds, not ports).

## 2. Kernel objects (xe_core.cpp)

```
struct XeExport { vnode_t vp; uint32_t vid; uint8_t kind; XeBo *bo; XeFence *f; uint32_t n; ... };   // key: (vp, vid)
```

- **dma-buf entry**: holds a BO reference (`boGet`). Import gives the caller a new GEM handle on the *same* `XeBo` in
  its client (`c->bos.add`, `boGet`), as `SURFACE_VRAM` already does for IOSurface backings, so binding, CPU maps
  (one cookie map per client, rb2's map-holds-BO rule) and freeing follow the BO refcount. The BO is marked
  `shared`: compressed PATs are refused for it from then on (Linux, xe_vm_bind_ioctl_validate_bo: no compression for
  imported dma-bufs; a CPU or another process reading it raw must see plain data) and it never moves
  (`noMove`, like a scan-out pin: another process may hold its pages mapped).
- **sync_file entry** (its stand-in file has size 0): a copy of the fences of a syncobj point at export time. Fences here are already device-global
  (slot, generation, seqno), valid in any client, so a copy is all a sync_file needs; `fenceSignaled()` and the ban
  floor (rb2) apply unchanged. Import: `syncReplace()` of the target syncobj (Linux `IMPORT_SYNC_FILE` = temporary
  payload) or a timeline point (`SYNCOBJ_FD_TO_HANDLE` with `IMPORT_SYNC_FILE` and a point).
- **syncobj fd (opaque)**: `SYNCOBJ_HANDLE_TO_FD` without the sync_file flag shares the syncobj itself (the same
  `XeSyncobj` in two clients). That needs a refcount on `XeSyncobj` and its lock moved from the client lock to its own
  (today a syncobj belongs to one client, under that client's lock). ANV uses opaque syncobj fds for
  `VK_EXTERNAL_SEMAPHORE_HANDLE_TYPE_OPAQUE_FD`; Wine prefers sync_file/opaque depending on the semaphore type.
- **implicit sync on a dma-buf** (`DMA_BUF_IOCTL_EXPORT_SYNC_FILE` / `IMPORT_SYNC_FILE`, used by ANV for WSI and by
  Wine's swapchain): the dma-buf entry carries a fence list with dma_resv rules: exactly the surface-fence registry
  that exists for IOSurface ids (`surfaceAttach` / `surfCollect`, WRITE/READ usage, 1024 live entries). The entry's key
  becomes the registry key instead of an IOSurface id.

## 3. New ioctls (uapi/intelxe_drm.h), all on the client connection

| ioctl | in | out | Linux equivalent |
|---|---|---|---|
| `INTELXE_EXPORT` | kind (dmabuf / syncfile / syncobj), handle (BO or syncobj), point, flags, fd (unlinked file) | 0 | PRIME_HANDLE_TO_FD, SYNCOBJ_HANDLE_TO_FD |
| `INTELXE_IMPORT` | fd, kind, target syncobj + point (sync_file) | GEM handle / syncobj handle | PRIME_FD_TO_HANDLE, SYNCOBJ_FD_TO_HANDLE |
| `INTELXE_DMABUF_SYNC` | fd, direction, usage (READ/WRITE), syncobj | 0 | DMA_BUF_IOCTL_EXPORT/IMPORT_SYNC_FILE |
| `INTELXE_SYNC_MERGE` | fd a, fd b, new fd | 0 | SYNC_IOC_MERGE |
| `INTELXE_FD_INFO` | fd | kind, size | telling a stand-in from any other file (xemac asks before routing an ioctl) |

`DRM_CAP_PRIME` then answers IMPORT|EXPORT, and `DRM_CAP_SYNCOBJ` already says yes.

## 4. Userspace (xemac in Mesa; Wine needs nothing of its own)

- `drmPrimeHandleToFD` / `drmSyncobjHandleToFD` / `...FDToHandle` and `ioctl(fd, DMA_BUF_IOCTL_*)` / `SYNC_IOC_MERGE`
  on a stand-in are routed to the ioctls above (`INTELXE_FD_INFO` tells a stand-in from any other fd).
- `lseek(dmabuf_fd, 0, SEEK_END)` works unchanged (the file is truncated to the BO size).
- `close()`, `dup()`, `fork()`, `SCM_RIGHTS` need nothing: the stand-in is a real fd.

## 5. What it costs / risks

- No new memory paths: an import is a second handle on an existing BO; everything rb2-rb6 made safe (BO refcounts,
  bind atomicity, ban floor, map-holds-BO, compression rules) applies as is.
- A process can pin another's VRAM only through an fd it was given (the Linux model).
- One open file per export (no disk space: unlinked, sparse). The per-process fd limit (256 soft by default on macOS)
  is the practical ceiling, as on Linux; Wine raises its limit at start.
- Entries outlive their last fd by up to one timer period (the check in section 1); their BO stays allocated that long.
- Not covered: `VK_EXT_external_memory_host` is unrelated (userptr already works); Metal/IOSurface sharing stays on
  the IOSurface-id path (SURFACE_VRAM), which is the right one between Metal and ANV processes.

## 6. Order of work

1. dma-buf export/import + BO `shared` rules (unblocks Wine's shared textures and DXGI swapchains).
2. sync_file export/import into syncobjs (unblocks `VK_KHR_external_semaphore_fd` SYNC_FD and fence fds).
3. dma-buf implicit sync (EXPORT/IMPORT_SYNC_FILE) on top of the surface-fence registry.
4. Opaque syncobj sharing (refcounted syncobjs) and merge. poll on a sync_file stays unsupported (section 1).
