# Game mode in IntelXe Manager

> Design note with its date (2026-11-13, branch `osguard`; the kernel lease of section 2 on branch `slpcboost` the
> same day): it records the plan and the state of that day, not the current status. The macOS update guard, built on the same branch: [`DESIGN-os-update-guard.md`](DESIGN-os-update-guard.md).

## 1. What macOS already does

macOS 14 and later turn **Game Mode** on by themselves when a game runs full screen. A game is an app whose
`Info.plist` puts it in the games category (`LSApplicationCategoryType` `public.app-category.games` or one of the
`public.app-category.*-games`); a game can opt out with `GCSupportsGameMode` false. Game Mode gives the game priority
on the CPU and GPU, lowers what background tasks may use, and doubles the Bluetooth sampling rate of controllers and
headphones. There is no public API to read whether it is on or to turn it on for another app.

Its GPU part works through Apple's own GPU drivers' scheduling. Nothing of it reaches a third-party accelerator: on
this stack Game Mode is CPU-side only, and it knows nothing of the Arc's clock. What this stack can add is the clock.

## 2. The GPU's lowest clock

The GuC's SLPC picks the GT clock between a floor and a ceiling. IntelXe has the knobs, in release builds:

- `debug.intelxe.slpc_min` and `debug.intelxe.slpc_max` (MHz, read-write, root): the floor and the ceiling SLPC is
  given (`kernel/IntelXe/xe_core.cpp` `slpcParams`; the floor defaults to 1200 MHz, Wa_14022085890, the ceiling to
  RP0, 2850 MHz on the B580; both are clamped to RPn..RP0);
- since sysman2 (13 Nov) a write of either is sent to the GuC at once while SLPC runs, and kept for every later SLPC
  start (`xeSlpcKnobWrite`; Level Zero sysman's `zesFrequencySetRange` writes them; DESIGN-level-zero.md 10.6);
- `debug.intelxe.step=17` sends them to the GuC now (`slpcStep`; step 17 is in the release list of `stepAllowed`,
  with the other steps "that set what Linux exposes at runtime"). It sends the floor, the ceiling, ignore-efficient,
  the strategies and the power profile, all from their current values.

The Power and app page's *GPU clock* writes the same floor to NVRAM for the next start (`intelxe-gpu-min-mhz`); game
mode changes it only in the running kernel. Choices: 2000 MHz, 2400 MHz (the default; the same as the *Performance*
setting), or the card's highest (3000, clamped to RP0 by `slpcParams`). It is never set above the user's ceiling
(`slpc_max`, the *Quiet* setting's 1800 MHz): `slpcParams` does not order the two, so the helper caps the floor.
A floor at or below the current one changes nothing.

What it should buy: frames that do not wait for the clock to rise after a short idle (frame-time spikes when a game
alternates light and heavy frames). **Not measured yet** (section 7). The *Fast GPU response for apps* switch (the
GuC low-latency hint, a file the Metal driver reads at an app's start) is a different knob, per queue; game mode
does not touch it: it is a persistent file, and its test notes a GPU fault after a long idle.

### The kernel lease: `debug.intelxe.slpc_boost` (built 2026-11-13, branch `slpcboost`)

The helper exists because the floor needs root and must not outlive the app. The kernel now offers a floor that needs
neither (`kernel/IntelXe/xe_slpcboost.h`, the glue in `xe_core.cpp` next to `slpcParams`):

- `debug.intelxe.slpc_boost` (int, `CTLTYPE_INT | CTLFLAG_RW | CTLFLAG_ANYBODY`): a write of N (MHz) asks for a floor of
  N for **10 s** after the write; the next write renews it (and may change N); **0** ends it at once. A read returns the
  lease's floor as the GuC gets it (clamped, 0 = no lease). `debug.intelxe.slpc_boost_ms` (read-only, anybody): ms left.
- The GuC gets the higher of the lease's floor and the administrator's (`slpc_min`): a lease never lowers the floor.
  It is sent as Linux v7.2 `xe_guc_pc.c` `pc_set_min_freq` sends a minimum (`IGNORE_EFFICIENT_FREQUENCY` = min < RPe,
  then `GLOBAL_MIN_GT_UNSLICE_FREQ_MHZ`), through `IntelXe::slpcMinSet`, which `slpcParams` (step 17, bring-up, GT
  reset, resume) uses too; `slpcParams` includes an active lease, so a GT reset during one keeps it.
- A kernel timer (thread call) ends the lease and sends `slpc_min` again, so a client that dies cannot leave it up.
- Counters: `debug.intelxe.stats`, line "slpc boost" (lease, ms left, the GuC's minimum, `slpc_min`, ceiling; grants,
  renewals, releases, expired, ended by sleep; refused for the rate and for a GT not ready; clamped; sends);
  `debug.intelxe.dump` has `slpc_boost` and `slpc_boost_ms`.

**Security bounds.** Any user may write it, so its effect is bounded to a power cost within the administrator's
settings:

| Bound | How |
|---|---|
| One lease for the GPU | a single state, not one per requester; the latest write wins (another user's write replaces the floor and the end) and a release by any user ends it for everyone; a client that renews every 5 s takes it again at its next renewal. Two users asking at once therefore get the later one's floor, never less than `slpc_min` and never more than the ceiling |
| Never above the ceiling | clamped to [RPn, `slpc_max` or RP0] (`slpcParams`' ceiling), again at every use, so lowering `slpc_max` during a lease lowers it too |
| Never below the administrator's floor | the GuC gets max(lease, `slpc_min`) |
| Rate limit | 10 requests (N > 0) per second, whoever makes them; `EBUSY` beyond (a renewal every few seconds needs one). A release (0) is always taken and does not count: it can only lower the clock (fixed 13 Nov after the night run, where a release right after the `EBUSY` was refused too and the lease ran its 10 s) |
| Not while the GT sleeps or resets | `EAGAIN` while suspended, in a GT reset, wedged or without SLPC (as `xe_guc_pc_set_min_freq_locked` answers `-EAGAIN`); a release is taken all the same, and a send the GT could not take is retried every 100 ms until the reset is over |
| Ends on sleep | `xeSuspend` ends it before the GuC's soft reset; the resume sends `slpc_min` |
| Bounded in time | 10 s after the last write; a timer, not the client, ends it |

Reads take no lock (a read must not wait for a bring-up); writes, the timer and the H2G run under `gDevLock`. Host
test: `kernel/IntelXe/tests/slpcboost_test.cpp` (bounds and clamp, grant, renew, the latest write wins, expiry,
release, the 5 s renewal pattern, the rate limit and a 1 kHz flood, a release after `EBUSY`, two users, a GT not
ready and the retry, sleep, `slpc_max` lowered during a lease).

**The app.** When the kext has the sysctl and the Time Machine option is off, game mode starts no helper and asks for
no password: the app writes the floor when a game comes to the front, every 5 s while it stays there, and 0 when it
leaves, when game mode is turned off and when the app quits (writes go through a serial queue off the main thread).
`EAGAIN` and `EBUSY` wait for the next renewal; any other error stops game mode with a message. After a sleep the next
renewal takes a new lease. With an older kext, or with the Time Machine option (`tmutil` needs root), the helper below
is used as before.

## 3. Background work

| Candidate | Possible without disabling it system-wide? | Resumes? | Used |
|---|---|---|---|
| Spotlight: `mdutil -i off /` | no: it turns indexing off for the volume and is kept in the volume's index settings; an app that dies leaves it off | only when turned on again | no |
| Spotlight: `taskpolicy -b -p <pid>` on `mds_stores` (darwin background) | yes, per process, until the process ends | `-B` | no: `mds_stores` already runs at background priority, `mdworker_shared` processes are short-lived (a new one is not affected), and macOS's Game Mode already lowers background work |
| Time Machine: `tmutil disable` | no: persistent | only when enabled again | no |
| Time Machine: `tmutil stopbackup` | yes: cancels the backup that is running, nothing else | backupd runs the next scheduled backup as usual (hourly); nothing to undo | yes, opt-in: while a game is in front the helper stops a backup that is running, checking every 10 s |

## 4. How it works

- **Opt-in, per session.** The Power and app page's *Game mode* switch is off at every start of the app; its
  choices (the clock, Time Machine, the list of added games) are kept, the switch is not. With the kernel lease (section
  2) that is all: no helper, no password. Otherwise turning it on asks for the administrator password once (`run()` with `osascript`, as the app's other changes) and starts
  `Resources/gamemode-helper.sh --run APP_PID UID FLOOR STOP_BACKUPS` as root in the background.
- **The helper** reads `debug.intelxe.slpc_min` (refuses to start without it), makes the pipe
  `/var/run/intelxe-gamemode/ctl` (mode 0600, owned by the user), writes its state next to it, and waits for one
  word per line: `game` sets the floor (and stops a Time Machine backup if asked), `desktop` puts the original floor
  back, `quit` ends. It also ends when the app's process is gone (checked every 2 s), on TERM or INT, and puts the
  floor back first (an EXIT trap). Arguments are fixed when it starts, through the password dialog; the pipe carries
  only those three words, so another process of the same user can at most switch between the two values the user
  approved. One helper at a time.
- **The app** follows the frontmost app (`NSWorkspace.didActivateApplicationNotification`). A game is an app in the
  games category or one the user added (bundle ID, or the executable's name for programs without a bundle: `java`
  for Minecraft). It sends `game` or `desktop` when that changes, and `quit` when game mode is turned off or the app
  quits. Full screen is not required (macOS's own Game Mode requires it; the clock helps a windowed game as much).
- **Undo.** Off: the switch, the menu bar item, quitting the app. Nothing is written to disk but the pipe and state
  in `/var/run`, which macOS empties at each start, as the kernel forgets the floor. The one case that leaves the
  floor raised is a helper killed with `kill -9` or crashed in a game: the app finds its state (a dead pid, phase
  `game`) and offers *Put it back* (`--restore`); a new helper restores it first too; a restart of macOS does as well.
- **The menu bar item** (opt-in, Monitor page): a line with the state ("Game mode: Minecraft in front"), *Turn game
  mode on…/off*, and *Count <app> as a game* for the last app in front that is not the Manager. Its icon turns into a
  game controller while a game is in front.

## 5. Files

`kernel/IntelXe/xe_slpcboost.h` and `xe_core.cpp` (the lease), `kernel/IntelXe/tests/slpcboost_test.cpp`,
`app/Resources/gamemode-helper.sh`, `app/Sources/GameMode.swift` (controller, Power and app section, menu lines),
`app/Sources/MenuBar.swift`, `app/Sources/main.swift` (the menu bar icon), `app/Sources/Settings.swift`,
`tools/report/collect-macos.sh` (the helper's state when one runs), `app/tests/test-gamemode-helper.sh`.

## 6. Tests

- `app/tests/test-gamemode-helper.sh` (about 30 s, no root, `sysctl` and `tmutil` stubbed in a throwaway root): bad
  arguments, no driver, refusal outside the test root without root; the pipe's mode; `game`, a repeated `game`,
  `desktop`, an unknown word; one helper at a time; the floor put back on `quit`, when the app process ends, on
  TERM; `kill -9` (the floor stays, `--status` says not running, `--restore` puts it back, a new helper restores
  first); the cap at the user's ceiling; a floor below the current one writes nothing; Time Machine left alone
  without the option and on the desktop, stopped in a game, and a backup that starts during the game stopped too.
- `IntelXeManager --selftest`: the games category, the list keys, the helper command's quoting, the state file; when
  the lease is used instead of the helper, the lease value in a game and on the desktop, which write errors pass, and
  no write without the sysctl.
- `kernel/IntelXe/tests/slpcboost_test.cpp`: the lease (section 2).

## 7. What needs the test machine (the night run)

- The lease as a user (no sudo): `sysctl -w debug.intelxe.slpc_boost=2400`, then `debug.intelxe.slpc_boost`,
  `slpc_boost_ms` and the stats line; the actual clock at idle (`debug.intelxe.sensors`) at or above 2400 MHz during
  the lease and back to the 1200 MHz floor 10 s after the last write (expiry) or at once after a write of 0 (release);
  a write of 3000 reads back 2850 (RP0) and, with `slpc_max=1800` set by root, 1800 (clamp); eleven writes in a second
  give `EBUSY` on the last, and a write of 0 right after it succeeds and reads back 0 (night of 13 Nov: refused before
  the fix); a sleep and wake end the lease (stats "ended by sleep"); `gt_reset=1` during a lease keeps it. The app
  with this kext: no password dialog, the floor in a game, released on the desktop.

- The helper with the real kext: `sysctl -w debug.intelxe.slpc_min=2400` and `step=17` while Metal clients run, and
  the clock read back (`debug.intelxe.sensors`, the Monitor page) in a game and after it.
- The effect: the Minecraft benchmark's frame times (average and 1 % low) with game mode off and on, and idle power
  in the game's menu (the floor costs power when the game waits).
- The password dialog, the menu bar lines, the frontmost-app switching, Time Machine with a real backup.

# Long-running VMs in IntelXe.kext (lrmode, 2026-11-12)

> Design note with its date: it records the plan and the state of that day, not the current status. Branch `lrmode`,
> **untested on hardware** (build and host tests only). Current status: `docs/ROADMAP.md`.

`DRM_XE_VM_CREATE_FLAG_LR_MODE` is what Intel's compute runtime (NEO) asks for on every VM
(`IoctlHelperXe::getFlagsForVmCreate`). Until this branch the kext refused it, so NEO ran in dma-fence VMs (compute
patch 0006's fallback) without its ring-buffer direct submission (ULLS, patch 0009), and a kernel running longer than
the job timeout (10 s, `debug.intelxe.job_timeout_ms`) was reset and its queue banned (DESIGN-level-zero.md, section 2,
"Blockers found" item 1). This note is what the kext does now, against Linux xe (v6.18+ tree in `dl/linux-xe`).

## 1. What Linux does

| Topic | Linux (file: function) |
|---|---|
| accepting the flag | `xe_vm.c: xe_vm_create_ioctl`: LR_MODE alone, or with FAULT_MODE (`has_usm`), NO_VM_OVERCOMMIT only with FAULT_MODE. Without FAULT_MODE the VM is in *preempt-fence mode* (`xe_vm.h: xe_vm_in_preempt_fence_mode`) |
| out-syncs | `xe_exec.c: xe_exec_ioctl` and `xe_vm.c: xe_vm_bind_ioctl` parse every sync with `SYNC_PARSE_FLAG_LR_MODE`; `xe_sync.c: xe_sync_entry_parse` answers `-EOPNOTSUPP` for a `SYNCOBJ` or `TIMELINE_SYNCOBJ` with `DRM_XE_SYNC_FLAG_SIGNAL`. In-syncs and user fences are allowed (uAPI doc of `drm_xe_vm_create`) |
| exec without batch | `xe_exec_ioctl`: `if (!xe_vm_in_lr_mode(vm))` around `xe_sync_in_fence_get` / `xe_sync_entry_signal`: on an LR VM nothing happens |
| exec and kernel fences | `xe_exec_ioctl` skips the drm_exec locking, the `DMA_RESV_USAGE_KERNEL` deps and `drm_gpuvm_resv_add_fence` for LR VMs: job fences are not in the BOs' dma-resv |
| job timeout | `xe_guc_submit.c: guc_exec_queue_init`: `timeout = MAX_SCHEDULE_TIMEOUT` when `q->vm` is in LR mode; `guc_exec_queue_timedout_job` asserts an LR job only gets there killed or after an error; `xe_exec_queue.c: xe_exec_queue_is_lr` (not for VM bind queues) |
| reset and ban | unchanged for LR: a GuC context reset or CAT error bans (`xe_guc_exec_queue_reset_trigger_cleanup`), a GT reset bans a queue whose first pending job started (`guc_exec_queue_stop`) |
| memory protection | `xe_vm.c: xe_vm_add_compute_exec_queue`: every exec queue of the VM has a preempt fence in the BOOKKEEP slot of the VM's resv (and of its external BOs, `drm_gpuvm_resv_add_fence`). Anything that waits for a BO to be idle (TTM eviction, `xe_bo.c: xe_bo_trigger_rebind`, `ttm_bo_release` of a freed BO or page table) enables those fences |
| preempting | `xe_preempt_fence.c: preempt_fence_enable_signaling` -> `q->ops->suspend` (`xe_guc_submit.c: __guc_exec_queue_process_msg_suspend`: a schedule disable of an enabled context, after it ran `min_run_period_lr_ms` (5 ms, `xe_device.c`) since its last resume); `preempt_fence_work_func` -> `suspend_wait` (`guc_exec_queue_wait_suspend_done`, 5 s; on timeout `guc_exec_queue_suspend_timeout_ban`), then the fence signals and the rebind worker is queued |
| resuming | `xe_vm.c: preempt_rebind_work_func`: revalidate and rebind what moved, `dma_resv_wait_timeout(KERNEL)` for the rebinds, then `resume_and_reinstall_preempt_fences` -> `q->ops->resume` (`__guc_exec_queue_process_msg_resume`: a schedule enable). Work submitted meanwhile only moved the ring tail (`submit_exec_queue` returns early for a suspended queue) |
| engine groups | `xe_hw_engine_group.c: xe_hw_engine_group_add_exec_queue` returns at once for preempt-fence-mode VMs; `xe_hw_engine_group_find_exec_mode` gives them `EXEC_MODE_DMA_FENCE`: only fault-mode VMs switch a group to LR mode, so without fault mode there is nothing to arbitrate |
| TLB | `xe_vm_create`: `batch_invalidate_tlb = false` for LR VMs |
| power | `xe_vm_create` takes a runtime-PM reference for an LR VM (no runtime suspend while it exists) |
| system sleep | `xe_pm.c: xe_pm_suspend`: `xe_bo_evict_all` (preempts LR queues through their fences), then `xe_gt_suspend` -> `xe_uc_stop` -> `xe_guc_submit_stop` -> `guc_exec_queue_stop`, which bans a queue whose job started and did not complete, LR or not |

## 2. What the kext does (`kernel/IntelXe/xe_core.cpp` "long-running VMs", pure logic in `xe_lr.h`)

- **VM_CREATE** (`xeVmCreateCheck`, `xe_uapi_args.cpp`): LR_MODE accepted, `XeVm::lr`. FAULT_MODE stays EINVAL (no GPU
  page-fault service; xe's answer on a device without `has_usm`), so NO_VM_OVERCOMMIT is EINVAL too.
- **EXEC / VM_BIND syncs**: `kXeSyncParseLrMode` on an LR VM (`xeSyncEntryCheck` had the rule since rb7). VM_BIND now
  looks the VM up before its syncs (EINVAL for an unknown VM, as `xe_vm_lookup`'s caller). An EXEC without batch on an
  LR VM does nothing (`xeLrExecNoop`); one on a banned queue is ECANCELED first, as `reset_status`.
- **Job timeout**: `watchRun` skips an LR VM's queues (`xeLrJobTimeoutApplies`), including the "never started" and
  "stuck after a GuC reset" rules (rb8d): Linux has no timer for them at all. A job that outlives the limit is counted
  once ("past the job timeout"). GuC context resets and GT resets still ban them (`queueKickOff`, `xeGtReset`).
- **Preemption** replaces the job waits that protect memory. Two users:
  - *Moves* (`boMove` with `mayWait`, which is the CPU-map path `boMakeVisible`, and `boMoveSys`): `lrHoldBegin` holds
    every LR VM that binds the BO; `lrMoveReady` takes each queue off (`lrQueueOff`, one `xeLrQueueStep` per call):
    `lrOff` keeps the ring closed (the FIFO keeps jobs; `queueExec`, the submit worker and direct submission all test
    it, as they test `tdr`), an armed direct-submission slot leaves first; a queue with work in its ring gets
    `SCHED_CONTEXT_MODE_SET(disable)` once 5 ms have passed since its last resume, and counts as off when
    `SCHED_CONTEXT_MODE_DONE` arrives; a queue with an idle ring needs no round trip. Then the copy and remap as before;
    `lrMoveDone` waits for the remap's TLB invalidation (the rebind worker's `dma_resv_wait` before the resume) and
    `lrHoldEnd` sends `SCHED_CONTEXT_MODE_SET(enable)` to each queue it disabled (`lrVmOn`) and kicks the FIFOs.
  - *Deferred frees* (`deferSealLr`): an unbind, a purge or a remap of an LR VM releases page tables and BO memory only
    after one **preemption cycle** of its queues instead of their jobs (which may never end: an endless ULLS ring would
    leak every unbind). The cycle is asked for only when a queue has work outstanding (the rule `deferJobsSnap` applies
    to dma-fence VMs: a job submitted after the seal starts with the PTEs gone and invalidates its TLB in the ring).
    `lrRequest` puts the VM on `gLrHead`; the submit worker (`lrRun`, every 2 ms while one is pending, kicked by
    `SCHED_CONTEXT_MODE_DONE`) takes the queues off the same way, counts the cycle done (`lrDone`, which the deferred
    entries compare with `xeLrCycleCovers`) and resumes them.
  - A disable not confirmed within 5 s bans the queue and, on the primary GT, resets the GT
    (`guc_exec_queue_suspend_timeout_ban`; the watchdog's rule for an unconfirmed disable). The queue still counts as
    running (`lrStuck`) until that reset has stopped the engines (or the disable is confirmed after all): no cycle
    completes and no move copies before. On the media GT, which the kext cannot reset, it stays so (memory kept rather
    than freed under a context that may still run). A move that gives up waiting leaves the VM to a cycle, which
    resumes it once every disable is confirmed (`lrVmSettled`).
  - A closed queue, or one `queueKickOff` takes off after a GuC reset, still counts until its own disable (teardown,
    watchdog) is confirmed or its ring is idle; the preemption sends it nothing. An LR queue's teardown disables it at
    once (xe's kill) instead of giving its jobs 2 s.
  - An enable that would go to a GuC that cannot take it (GT reset in progress, the wake before `gSuspended` clears)
    waits: the VM stays listed and the submit worker sends it once the GuC is back, so a queue registered disabled at
    the wake is never left disabled.
  - Holds and cycles stack (`xeLrResumeNow`: no resume while a hold or a requested cycle remains), as xe's
    `suspend_count`.
  - A GT reset or a wake from sleep registers a held queue **disabled** and marks it confirmed off; the resume's enable
    then runs what its ring holds (Linux: `submit_exec_queue` returns early for a suspended queue). The replay's
    `SCHED_CONTEXT` is not sent for it.
- **Evictions and purges** (`evictClient`, `boMove` without `mayWait`, `purgeBlocked`) still take only BOs whose VMs are
  idle: an eviction does not wait, so a busy LR VM's window BOs stay (as a busy dma-fence VM's do), and the map that
  needed the room moves its own BO to system memory if the window is full (`boMoveSys`, which does preempt).
- **System sleep**: unchanged. `xeSuspend` waits 2 s for the queues and bans those still running: Linux bans a started
  LR job in `guc_exec_queue_stop` after `xe_bo_evict_all` suspended it, so both end with the queue banned (NEO reports
  a lost device after the wake, as on Linux). VRAM is saved and restored in place (same DPAs), so no rebind is needed.
  No preemption runs during sleep (`xeSuspend` holds every client lock, so no move is in progress; a pending cycle
  waits for the GuC, `kXeLrWaitGuc`, and completes after the wake).
- **TLB**: `tlbFlushDue` never applies the on-demand per-batch rule (`tlb_every_batch`) to an LR VM.
- **Teardown** of an LR queue does not wait 2 s for its jobs.
- **Counters**: `debug.intelxe.stats`, line "long-running VMs (lrmode)": VMs made; live and held queues; execs (and
  those without batch); out-syncs refused; jobs past the job timeout; disables, enables, unconfirmed (banned); cycles
  asked, done, pending; move holds, how many waited and how long (mean, max); invalidations still pending at a resume.

### Where the kext differs from xe, and why

| Item | xe | kext | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| kernel fences on exec | not waited for on an LR VM | still waited (`vm->kern`, the clears of fresh VRAM) | xe's LR bind job waits for the BO's clear before writing the PTEs; here VM_BIND writes the PTEs in the ioctl and the exec's wait is what keeps a batch from reading VRAM before its clear |
| what is preempted for a free | every free of a BO or page table on the VM's resv (TTM) | only when a queue of the VM has work outstanding | an idle queue cannot be translating through the removed PTEs, and its next job invalidates first; saves a GuC round trip per unbind of an idle VM |
| queue with an idle ring | disabled anyway when enabled | held (ring closed) without a disable | nothing of it can run until the hold ends |
| rebind | a worker revalidates evicted BOs and rebinds them on the GPU | the move rewrites the PTEs on the CPU itself (`boRemap`) | binds are CPU page-table writes here; the queues are off for exactly the copy, remap and invalidation |
| evictions | TTM evicts LR BOs by preempting | only idle VMs' BOs | an eviction here never waits; the mapping path preempts instead |
| runtime PM | an LR VM holds a runtime-PM reference | nothing | the kext has no runtime D3 |

## 3. Direct submission (debug.intelxe.direct) and LR queues

The kext's own direct submission and NEO's ULLS are independent: ULLS is one exec of NEO's ring buffer, a batch that
spins on a semaphore in user memory and never ends while NEO keeps it running. With LR VMs that job is exempt from the
watchdog, so ULLS can run (patch 0009 lets NEO turn it on once the kext accepts LR_MODE). The kext's slot arms only
after two execs within `direct_idle_us`, so a ULLS queue (one exec) normally never arms; a slot armed behind a job that
does not end is harmless (it runs after the job, or its no-op does when the idle exit fires). An LR queue that is not
running ULLS (NEO with `EnableDirectSubmission=0`, any other user) arms and leaves exactly as a dma-fence queue does:
the idle exit, contention, a FIFO wait, suspend, GT reset, close. The one new exit is the LR preemption: `lrQueueOff`
makes an armed queue leave before it closes the ring (counted as "other"), since a held queue's FIFO must take the
jobs and an armed queue's FIFO must stay empty; `dsEnter` and `dsSubmit` refuse a held queue. An LR queue is not kept
armed past the idle exit: Linux has no kernel-side direct submission for user queues (its `xe_ring_ops.c` ULLS is the
migrate queue's), and a context that polls when nothing comes costs power (+7 W measured, DESIGN-direct-submission.md)
and keeps other contexts waiting for a timeslice.

## 4. Tests

- Host: `kernel/IntelXe/tests/lr_test.cpp` (55 checks: VM_CREATE flags, the sync rules, the preemption step and a
  whole multi-queue preemption, cycle counters, resume rules), with the other host tests unchanged.
  `c++ -std=c++17 -Wall -Wextra -I.. -o lr_test lr_test.cpp ../xe_uapi_args.cpp && ./lr_test`
- GPU: `user/tests/kernel/lr.c`, phases `args`, `long`, `ds` (see its header). Build on the build Mac:
  `clang -arch x86_64 -O2 -I../../../kernel/IntelXe/uapi -o lr lr.c -framework IOKit`.

Night commands (test machine, the kext from this branch installed; each ≤ 60 s):

```sh
./lr args                                            # < 1 s: the uAPI rules
./lr long                                            # job_timeout_ms + 2 s (13 s by default): no TDR, the move and cycle
./lr ds                                              # < 1 s, only with debug.intelxe.direct=1 (the default in the tree)
sysctl debug.intelxe.stats | grep -E "long-running|^TDR|^jobs|^BO moves|direct submission"
./ufence && ./unbindfence && ./bomove && ./bomove evict   # dma-fence VMs unchanged
# NEO in LR mode with ULLS (DESIGN-level-zero.md section 9 for the setup):
cd ~/l0/builtins && DYLD_LIBRARY_PATH=$HOME/l0/lib NEOReadDebugKeys=1 PrintXeLogs=1 ../bin/ze_hello kernel ../kernels/fill_ids_bmg.bin 2>&1 | grep -iE "LongRunning|ze_hello|error" | tail -20
```

On a failure: `log show --last 2m --predicate 'sender == "IntelXe"' | tail -60` (the G2H log has the "LR preemption"
lines) and the stats line above.

## 5. Open items

- Untested on the B580: whether a GuC schedule disable takes a context polling `MI_SEMAPHORE_WAIT` off promptly (it
  must: NEO's ULLS on Linux depends on it, and i915's timeslicing relied on semaphore waits being preemption points);
  `./lr long` shows it (move hold wait in the stats line).
- Preemption granularity: a context polling a semaphore or between batches leaves the engine at once, but a running
  compute walker leaves at a thread-group boundary until the SIP kernel exists (compute patch 0008: thread-group
  preemption without a compiler). A thread group that runs longer than the 640 ms preemption timeout makes the GuC
  reset the engine, and the queue is banned, as on Linux without mid-thread preemption. Moves and frees of a busy LR
  VM are where that can now happen; mid-thread preemption (SIP, IGC on macOS) removes it.
- A move whose remap invalidation is not answered within the TLB fence timeout resumes the queues anyway (counted
  "invalidation late at resume"); the old blocks are still freed only after it, as for every unanswered invalidation
  the kext counts done, but GPU writes through a stale entry would land in the old copy.
- Error order: an EXEC on a banned LR queue with invalid syncs answers the sync error first (xe: ECANCELED first).
- Evictions of busy LR VMs' window BOs (xe preempts for them); purges of DONTNEED BOs in busy LR VMs.
- A preemption cycle per unbind of a busy VM is xe's behaviour too, but NEO frees often: measure the disable/enable
  rate under a real Level Zero workload (stats line) before tuning (batching frees per cycle already happens: one cycle
  covers every free asked for while it runs).
- Fault mode (`FAULT_MODE`, SVM, `CPU_ADDR_MIRROR`) remains refused.

# Metal mesh pipelines with an object stage on the B580

Branch fix016, 14 November 2026. Plugin `nullmoth/plugin/NVMTLLibraryLoad.m` ("batch 42a"), translator
`nullmoth/translator/translator/src/mesh_lower.rs`.

## What 0.1.5 did

Mesh shading is emulated with compute, as nullmoth did on NVK: the mesh function is lowered (AIR to AIR) into a kernel
that writes each threadgroup's vertices, primitive attributes, indices and primitive count into a block of a scratch
buffer, and a generated vertex function (`m2v_mesh_vs`) draws the blocks. With an object stage the object function is
lowered into a kernel too: it writes its grid and payload into a per-object record and raises, with atomic max, the
header the GPU then reads: the indirect dispatch of the mesh kernel (`threadgroups x objects x 1`, bytes 0-11) and the
indirect draw (`vertex count, objects as instances`, bytes 16-31). Layout of the scratch:

| bytes | content |
| --- | --- |
| 0-63 | header: dispatch arguments (0), objects (4), draw arguments (16) |
| 64 - 64 + block | the block dead threadgroups write into |
| `tr` + o x `rs` | object o's record: its grid (16 bytes), then its payload |
| `tr` + objects x `rs` + (o x cap + j) x block | mesh threadgroup j of object o |

On 13 November an object + mesh pipeline (`mtl_desc_paths` "mesh") ran 20 s on the B580 and the device was lost
("vk: slowest submit so far 20348 ms ... GPU RECOVERY", one GuC context reset). 0.1.5 refused such pipelines with an
`NSError` (code 42) instead; `NVMTL_MESH_OBJECT=1` built them.

## The cause

Not the object stage. The mesh lowering rebases the mesh handle of every `air.set_*_mesh` call in the entry onto
`%m2v.mesh` (the scratch plus this threadgroup's block offset) by matching the argument text: `<type> %h` and
`<type> nocapture %h`, the forms of the typed-pointer compilers its fixtures came from. Metal's compiler on macOS 26
writes `ptr addrspace(7) captures(none) %m.coerce`, so the handle was never rebased and every store went relative to
the scratch's start: every mesh threadgroup wrote its block at offset 0. Vertex 0's position landed on bytes 16-31, the
indirect draw's arguments: the draw read float bits as its vertex and instance counts (about 3.2 x 10^9 and 1 x 10^9
for the test's quad) and ran until the GuC reset the context. Reproduced off the device: the test's shaders compiled on
an Apple GPU Mac (`libraryDataContents`), decoded with `nvmtl-air-dis`, lowered with the host-built translator (7336-byte
kernel and 2756-byte vertex SPIR-V, the sizes the B580 log shows): three of the four mesh stores went through
`%m.coerce`.

The same bug hit the other two modes: a mesh pipeline without an object stage drew every threadgroup into block 0 (one
quad visible; right only for a one-threadgroup draw), and `drawMeshThreadgroupsWithIndirectBuffer:` overwrote its
header like the object path.

## The fix

- `rebase_handle` rebases `<type> [parameter attributes] %h` followed by `,` or `)` whatever the attributes
  (`nocapture`, `captures(none)`, `noundef`, `align 16`, ...). Output for the typed-pointer fixtures is byte-identical.
- A `set_*` call in the entry whose handle is not `%m2v.mesh` after that is refused with an error naming it, instead of
  being lowered relative to an arbitrary pointer: a form the lowering does not know can no longer write over the header.
  (In a helper function the handle is the helper's own argument, which the entry passes as `%m2v.mesh`: unchanged.)
- The plugin builds object + mesh pipelines again; `NVMTL_MESH_OBJECT=0` refuses them as 0.1.5 did.

Other translations do not go through `mesh_lower.rs` (only `nvmtl_lower_mesh`/`nvmtl_lower_mesh2` call it): a sample of
247 corpus modules under `~/hackintosh/work` translated byte-identically with the translator before and after.

## Native task and mesh shaders (VK_EXT_mesh_shader)

ANV exposes `VK_EXT_mesh_shader` on the B580 (task and mesh shaders; the CTS `dEQP-VK.mesh_shader` group ran with no
failures in the 4 November run). It was not used here because a task shader can only feed a native mesh shader: the
object stage alone cannot be native while the mesh stage stays the compute emulation. Going native means a second
backend for both stages:

- the translator emitting `TaskEXT` / `MeshEXT` entry points (`OutputVertices`, `OutputPrimitivesEXT`,
  `OutputTrianglesEXT`/lines/points, `LocalSize`), per-vertex and per-primitive output arrays with the fragment
  function's locations, `PrimitiveTriangleIndicesEXT` and `CullPrimitiveEXT`;
- Metal's model rewritten to SPIR-V's: Metal lets any thread call `set_primitive_count` at any point and write outputs
  before it, while `OpSetMeshOutputsEXT` must come first, once, in uniform control flow (outputs buffered in workgroup
  memory and copied out after a barrier); `set_threadgroups_per_grid` from one object thread becomes
  `OpEmitMeshTasksEXT`, which every invocation must reach and which ends the task shader (the grid kept in workgroup
  memory until the end);
- the payload as a `TaskPayloadWorkgroupEXT` variable (`maxTaskPayloadSize`), and the mesh grid limits checked against
  `maxMeshWorkGroupCount`;
- the plugin creating graphics pipelines with task and mesh stages (descriptor and push-constant layouts with the
  `TASK`/`MESH` stage bits in both descriptor models) and drawing with `vkCmdDrawMeshTasksEXT` / `...IndirectEXT`
  (which would also give the object stage indirect draws, still "batch 42c" in the emulation).

That is the route to take for speed (no scratch round trip, no render-pass split per draw); the emulation is kept
because it is correct now and every piece of it runs on paths the rest of the driver already uses.

## Tests

- Translator: `a_handle_with_captures_none_writes_the_threadgroups_block_in_every_mode` (direct, indirect and object
  modes on the current compiler's output: `testdata/mesh_captures_*.ll`), `rebase_handle_skips_any_parameter_attributes_
  and_leaves_other_values`, `a_mesh_intrinsic_on_another_handle_is_refused_not_written_over_the_header`; the 25 earlier
  `mesh_lower` tests unchanged. 28/28.
- `user/tests/metal/mtl_mesh_object` (on a device; `--any` on an Apple GPU as the reference, 4/4 on the M1 Pro):
  object-rows (four object threadgroups launching 0, 1, 2 and 1 x 3 mesh threadgroups, payload colour and row, mesh
  bytes and a mesh buffer), object-redraw (two draws in one encoder, the second with other bindings and a mesh buffer
  offset), mesh-grid (4 x 2 threadgroups without an object stage), mesh-indirect (3 x 1 x 1 from a buffer at offset 16).
- Night phase M (`user/tests/metal/night-meshobj.sh`): those in both descriptor models, `mtl_desc_paths mesh`, the
  `NVMTL_MESH_OBJECT=0` switch, `mtl_smoke`, and the GuC reset counters before and after.

# Accelerating more than one display head (NMXAccel, NMXAGDC) — design

> Status (12 Nov 2026): implemented behind the multi-head knob (boot-arg `nmxheads=1`, NVRAM `nmx-heads=1`, or
> `debug.nmxaccel_heads_auto=1` at run time), default off, **untested with two heads**: the test machine has one monitor.
> With the knob off nothing new runs, except that the boot arm leaves IntelXeFB's second framebuffer (published at
> IntelXeFB's start with `-intelxefb_pipeb`) for `debug.nvaccelfb=3`, as it did a late head; with one head (no
> `-intelxefb_pipeb`) nothing new runs at all. The diagnostics `debug.nmxaccel_heads` and `debug.nmxagdc_heads`
> work with one monitor. The second head itself is IntelXeFB's ([`DESIGN-second-pipe.md`](DESIGN-second-pipe.md)).
> Since 12 Nov IntelXeFB publishes it at its start, disconnected (section 5, done); its one-monitor check is
> DESIGN-second-pipe.md §7.

## 1. How the accelerator binds to framebuffers today

* **One accelerator per GPU, several displays.** NMXAccel (`nullmoth/kexts/NVRM/accel/nvrm-accel.cpp`, an
  `IOGraphicsAccelerator2` on the B580's PCI device) has one display machine (`NVDisplayMachine`, an
  `IOAccelLegacyDisplayMachine`). The display machine owns one `IOAccelDisplayPipe` per IOFramebuffer it was handed with
  `found_framebuffer` (pipe table at display machine + 0x88, count at + 0x108; a pipe's framebuffer at pipe + 0x98).
  This is the shape nullmoth's NVIDIA driver was written for: `kNvMaxFB` = 5 heads (four NVIDIA heads and an Intel
  built-in panel), `populateAccelConfig` reports 5 framebuffers, and the Metal device is one per GPU, not per display.
* **Heads.** `fbPublished` (an `IntelXeFramebuffer` first-publish notification, so it also sees a head that publishes
  after NMXAccel started) slots each framebuffer by its `IOFBDependentIndex` into `fFBs[]`. Everything on the frame path
  is already per head: `pipeFramebuffer` maps a pipe back to its head by framebuffer pointer, `performTransaction`
  copies into *that* head's `nvScanoutInfo` surface, the async present state (`gNmxAs[head]`), the adaptive-sync window
  (`gNmxVrr[head]`) and the frame counters (`gCntIopOkHead[head]`) are per head.
* **The arm.** `nmxAutoArm` (boot1) waits for NMXAGDC's device control and for head 0 to go quiet, then writes levels
  1/3/4 through IntelXeFB's `intelxefbRunGated` (IOGraphics' system and controller gates, the order that does not
  deadlock against AppleGPUWrangler). Level 1 is `registerPendingLocked`: it walks indices 0, 1, 2, ... and calls
  `found_framebuffer` for every published head that has no pipe yet, stopping at the first index that has not published;
  then `display_mode_will_change`/`did_change` (the family enables the accelerator there). A head that publishes **after**
  that walk is only logged ("gets a pipe only when debug.nvaccelfb=3 is written again, and WindowServer composites it
  only after a WindowServer restart").

## 2. What IOGraphics, IOAccelerator and WindowServer expect of a multi-display GPU

* **IOGraphics** (SDK `IOKit/graphics/IOFramebuffer.h`, `IOGraphicsTypes.h`): the framebuffers of one controller share
  `kIOFBDependentIDKey` and are ordered by `kIOFBDependentIndexKey`; one IOFramebuffer stands for one CRTC/output. A
  display arriving or leaving is a *connection change* of an existing framebuffer: `kConnectionCheckEnable` /
  `kConnectionEnable` answered from the hardware, and `kIOFBConnectInterruptType` ("the display connection should be
  resensed") to make IOGraphics probe it again.
* **Apple's own drivers publish every framebuffer at start, connected or not.** On Intel Macs the `AppleIntelFramebuffer@0`
  .. `@N` nodes exist with nothing plugged in; AMD's controller publishes one framebuffer per display path the same way.
  The number of framebuffers on one GPU never changes at run time; what changes is their connection state. (An eGPU is
  not a counter-example: it is a new GPU with its own accelerator, AGDC and framebuffers.)
* **IOAcceleratorFamily2**: one accelerator per GPU; the display machine's start sweeps the GPU's framebuffers and makes
  a pipe for each (`IOAccelDisplayMachine::start`, `found_framebuffer`), and each pipe subscribes to its own
  framebuffer's notifications: `IOFramebuffer.h` reserves the notification group `kIOFBNotifyGroupID_AppleIOAccelDisplayPipe`
  (0x170), and `IOAccelDisplayPipe.h` has the receivers (`framebuffer_will_power_off`, `framebuffer_did_power_on`,
  `displayModeWillChange`/`DidChange`, `framebuffer_terminated`). So a head's mode changes, power and termination reach
  its pipe without NMXAccel's help once the pipe exists.
* **WindowServer / IOPresentment** builds its display pipes from AppleGraphicsDeviceControl command 0x980 (the list of
  framebuffers, NMXAGDC's reply) **when WindowServer starts**, then asks 0x921 (link configuration) and 0x711 (plane
  scaler, gamma, ... per framebuffer index). CoreDisplay logs "Unable to find display pipe for IOFB service" for a
  framebuffer that is not in that list, and never sends it a frame. nullmoth's field experience (the comment over
  `nvdaAgdcRescanForReply`): a monitor plugged in after boot was missing from the reply; with the rescan the reply is
  current, but only a WindowServer start asks for it again.
* **Consequence.** No restart is needed for a head that exists when WindowServer starts: plugging and unplugging its
  monitor is a connection change. A framebuffer that is *published* after WindowServer started can be armed on the
  accelerator at once (its pipe exists, frames would flow), but WindowServer composites it only after it rebuilds its
  display pipes (logout/login restarts WindowServer). That is the protocol's limit, not NMXAccel's; the way around it is
  to publish the head early (section 5).

## 3. What NMXAccel does with the knob on

* **Late heads** (`headsLate`, a thread call): a head (index ≥ 1) that publishes after the arm is registered 2 s later
  (never from inside the publish notification: that runs in the publisher's `registerService`, under IntelXeFB's pipe-B
  lock). Before: the head must go quiet (5 s) and describe its scan-out (`nvScanoutInfo`); otherwise it is retried every
  2 s for 30 s. Then, inside IOGraphics' gates through head 0's `intelxefbRunGated` (the second framebuffer is on the same
  controller), `registerPendingLocked` gives it its pipe. Mode `1` delivers the family-wide mode change the boot arm and
  `debug.nvaccelfb=3` deliver; mode `2` registers only and leaves the new pipe's mode changes to its own framebuffer
  notification (which of the two WindowServer wants is a two-monitor question). Never ungated: without the gate it is
  left for `debug.nvaccelfb=3`. The boot arm itself also kicks the late check once it is done, for a head that published
  while it ran.
* **Head 1 from the start** (12 Nov): with `-intelxefb_pipeb` IntelXeFB publishes its second framebuffer at its start,
  disconnected (`IntelXeFBConnected` false), so it is there for the boot arm. Knob on, the boot arm's walk registers it
  with head 0 (section 5); after the arm a disconnected head is registered without waiting for its scan-out (there is
  none to wait for). Knob off, the boot walk stops before an `IntelXeFramebufferPipe` (`nmxHeadBootSkips`, only while
  `nmxAutoArm`'s levels 1/3/4 run): it waits for `debug.nvaccelfb=3`, exactly as a late head did. (IOAcceleratorFamily's
  own sweep at NMXAccel's start may still give it a pipe if both heads published before NMXAccel started: that is the
  family's, not NMXAccel's, and `debug.nmxaccel_heads` shows it in the pipe table.)
* **The rule** is one pure function, `nmxHeadVerdict` in `nmx_heads.h`, shared by the late arm and the diagnostic and
  checked on the host (`tests/nmx_heads_test.cpp`, run by `build-intelxe.sh tests`): absent / armed (own pipe) /
  armed (own pipe) with no monitor (idle) / registered without a pipe / the pending boot arm takes it / the late arm
  takes it now / once its scan-out is up / manual (knob off: today's behaviour, also for the second framebuffer at the
  boot arm) / the accelerator is not armed at all (held, failed: nothing registers a head on its own) / blocked by a hole
  below it / terminated. Head 0 is never the late arm's. Inputs per head: published, registered, piped, scan-out,
  terminated, second-pipe framebuffer (`kNmxCapPipeFB`), and disconnected (`IntelXeFBConnected` false; absent means
  connected, as for head 0).
* **Termination**: a head ≥ 1 whose framebuffer terminates (IntelXeFB's stop takes the second framebuffer down) frees its
  slot and its published/registered/piped bits, so a new framebuffer at that index is registered again. Its reference is
  kept (a transaction in flight may hold the pointer), as `fbPublished` does for a displaced head 0. The pipe's own
  `framebuffer_terminated` is the family's.
* **Per-head capabilities**, read from the framebuffer's properties when it publishes (`nmxHeadCapsOf`); with the knob on a
  head ≥ 1 is never asked for what it lacks. Head 0 is never skipped, whatever its properties say.

| capability | head 0 (`IntelXeFramebuffer`) | head 1 (`IntelXeFramebufferPipe`) | what NMXAccel does for head 1 |
|---|---|---|---|
| flips (`IntelXeFBScanoutVersion`, `nmxScanout`) | yes | no | copy only: no flip, no "home" after a copy. Scan-out bindings are pinned and mapped by head 0's framebuffer at head 0's size, so they could never be head 1's anyway |
| pipe gamma (`IntelXeFBPipeGammaSize`, `nmxPipeGamma`) | yes | no | no table sent. NMXAGDC offers the 0x711 gamma capability only to a head with the property, so CoreDisplay applies gamma in its own GPU pass for head 1 |
| AGDC timing (`NVRMTiming`) | yes | yes (IntelXeFB hook, below) | NMXAGDC answers 0x921 and the plane scaler for index 1 |
| adaptive-sync stamps (`nmxVrrStamp`) | yes | no | asked once, refused, logged once (unchanged) |
| cursor | IntelXeFB's cursor plane (or software, `debug.intelxefb_hwcursor`) | software: `kIOHardwareCursorAttribute` 0 | nothing: WindowServer draws the cursor into head 1's composite |

* **Cursor and scaler per head.** The hardware cursor and its coordinate space (`fCurSpaceW/H` for a scaled HiDPI mode)
  belong to the framebuffer, and only head 0 has a cursor plane. The scaler state that matters to the accelerator is
  the plane-scaler capability NMXAGDC answers per head from that head's own `NVRMTiming`: the head's size at 1:1
  (0x10001, b580-hidpi finding 5), so WindowServer scales any scaled mode on the GPU and presents frames at the head's
  scan-out size. Per head, `debug.nmxaccel_heads` shows the last copied frame's source size against the scan-out size and
  counts mismatches (the "source 2560x1440 is not the scanout's" refusal), which is how a head whose scaling went to the
  pipe would show.
* **Display pipe capabilities.** `IOAccelDisplayPipeCapabilities` is one property of the accelerator (one device, one
  plane, two queued transactions); `IOAccelDisplayPipe::copyCapabilities` returns it for every pipe, which describes each
  pipe correctly. Whether IOPresentment wants one device entry per framebuffer instead is open (two monitors).

## 4. NMXAGDC: listing IntelXeFB's heads

* The 0x980 reply already lists every `IntelXeFramebuffer` under the B580 by `IOFBDependentIndex` (rescanned at most once
  a second when WindowServer asks, so a head published after boot is in the next reply), `portMask` bit 1 + i,
  `maxFramebuffers` = the number of heads without a hole. 0x921 and 0x711 are answered per index from that head's
  `NVRMTiming` (link port 1 + index), the gamma capability only for a head with `IntelXeFBPipeGammaSize`.
* A disconnected head is listed like any other (Apple's model: every framebuffer of the GPU is in the reply), with
  IntelXeFB's placeholder timing (CEA 1920x1080@60) or the last monitor's as its `NVRMTiming`, so 0x921/0x711 for its
  index are answered rather than refused (a refused link query was the single-head "0x80e" symptom). The dry run
  prints each head's monitor state.
* New: a head ≥ 1 publishing brings nothing up (the device control comes up from head 0; before, the second framebuffer
  logged "publishes no IntelXeFBAccelAllowed"), and the dry run `debug.nmxagdc_heads`: what the next 0x980 would list,
  scanned into a table of its own (the live table is not touched), each head's K5 answers (timing, plane scaler, gamma),
  whether it is in the live table yet (no: WindowServer has not asked since it published), and what IOPresentment asked.
* **IntelXeFB hook** (`kernel/IntelXeFB/IntelXeFB.cpp`, `IntelXeFramebufferPipe::configure`, a few lines): the second
  framebuffer publishes `NVRMTiming` (same layout as `publishTiming`: tag, pixel clock in Hz, h/v visible, sync start, sync
  end, total, refresh in mHz, sync polarities) and `NVRMFlipWaitUs` (a frame and a quarter). Without `NVRMTiming`,
  IOPresentment's 0x921 for index 1 was refused ("Unable to acquire capabilities ... 0x80e" was the single-head symptom
  of a missing link answer), and head 1's present wait fell back to 8 ms. Only under `-intelxefb_pipeb`: the second
  framebuffer exists nowhere else.

## 5. A second monitor without a WindowServer restart: head 1 published at start (done 12 Nov)

IntelXeFB publishes `IntelXeFramebufferPipe` at its start whenever `-intelxefb_pipeb` is on (and the panel is on pipe A),
disconnected: `kConnectionCheckEnable`/`kConnectionEnable` 0, the offline mode (`kIOTimingIDApple_0x0_0hz_Offline`) as
its one mode, a placeholder `NVRMTiming`, `nvScanoutInfo` answering not-ready, `IntelXeFBConnected` false. A sink
arriving or leaving is `configure` + `setConnected` plus the connect interrupt (IOGraphics' side, with the SDK header
and IOGraphics source references: [`DESIGN-second-pipe.md`](DESIGN-second-pipe.md) §3). That is Apple's model
(section 2):

* IOGraphics has both framebuffers in `gStartedFramebuffers` before its first open, so it links them as one
  controller's dependents and opens head 1 with head 0; head 1 is offline, so it gets no `IODisplay` and WindowServer
  shows no display for it.
* NMXAGDC's first 0x980 (WindowServer's start) lists both heads (`debug.nvrmfb_agdc_maxfb` 2), and K5 answers for
  index 1 from the placeholder timing.
* With the knob, NMXAccel's boot arm registers head 1 with head 0 (section 3): its display pipe exists before
  WindowServer starts. A head armed while disconnected gets no framebuffer resource (`initFramebufferResource` refuses a
  scan-out that does not describe itself, the family's own default) until its first mode change, which its pipe's
  framebuffer notification delivers once WindowServer sets the new monitor's mode.
* A monitor plugged in later is then a connection change WindowServer handles live; unplugging it reports the head
  disconnected and leaves it published. Knob off, NMXAccel leaves the head unregistered (`debug.nvaccelfb=3`), so a
  monitor is listed by WindowServer but gets frames only after that step.

Open (two monitors): whether IOPresentment re-reads the plane-scaler capability (0x711) when the monitor arrives or keeps
the placeholder's 1920x1080 from WindowServer's start; whether the family's `found_framebuffer` gives a disconnected
framebuffer a pipe (the one-monitor night check answers this one: head 1 "armed (own display pipe), no monitor" versus
"registered, NO pipe of its own"); mode 1 against mode 2 of the knob no longer matters for head 1 at boot (the boot
arm delivers the mode change itself).

## 6. Knobs and sysctls

| name | kind | default | meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `nmxheads=N` (boot-arg) / `nmx-heads` (NVRAM, "0".."2") | knob | 0 | 1: late heads registered with the mode change; 2: registered without it; 0: off |
| `debug.nmxaccel_heads_auto` | int, rw | the knob | the same at run time; writing 1 or 2 also runs the late check now |
| `debug.nmxaccel_heads` | string, ro, root | — | every head: class, registry id, index, scan-out, capabilities, cursor, frames, last source vs scan-out size, late registration, and the verdict; the display machine's pipe → head table; the late arm's last result. No register writes, no registration, no kernel pointers |
| `debug.nmxagdc_heads` | string, ro | — | NMXAGDC's dry run (section 4) |

## 7. Tests

* Host: `build-intelxe.sh tests` builds and runs `nmx_heads_test` (49 checks of the verdict, the boot-walk skip and the
  capability rule).
* One monitor (nights): `sudo sysctl -n debug.nmxaccel_heads` and `sudo sysctl -n debug.nmxagdc_heads` with the knob off
  (head 0 armed with its own pipe, head 1 absent, NMXAGDC would list one head with a 2560x1440 link timing); then
  `sudo sysctl -w debug.nmxaccel_heads_auto=1`, the same reads (knob 1, "nothing to register", head 0's frame count still
  growing, desktop unchanged), then `=0`. A boot with NVRAM `nmx-heads=1`: the same, and the log's `multi-head:` lines.
* One monitor with head 1 published at start (`intelxefb-pipeb=1` and `nmx-heads=1`): DESIGN-second-pipe.md §7 has the
  exact commands and expected output (head 1 "armed (own display pipe), no monitor", NMXAGDC listing two heads,
  `system_profiler` one display).
* Two monitors (open): `-intelxefb_pipeb` and `nmx-heads=1`; boot with one monitor, plug the second in after login:
  head 1's verdict goes "armed (own display pipe), no monitor" → "armed (own display pipe)", its frame count in
  `debug.nmxaccel_heads` grows, a second desktop appears without a logout (`debug.nvrmfb_agdc_maxfb` stays 2); unplug/replug
  of the second monitor (the head stays published, its scan-out answers not-ready while disconnected); both monitors at
  boot; a system sleep with both (no connection report at the wake for the same monitor); IntelXeFB's stop
  (termination frees the slot).

# The macOS update guard: IntelXe Manager before and after a macOS update

> Design note with its date (2026-11-13, branch `osguard`): it records the plan and the state of that day, not the
> current status. Game mode, built on the same branch, has its own note: [`DESIGN-game-mode.md`](DESIGN-game-mode.md).

A macOS update replaces the system volume and the kernel collections Apple ships. Part of this stack lives there or
is linked against it. Until now the user guide (`site/guide/upgrading.html`, `release/README-INSTALL.md` "If it does
not come up") said what to do afterwards, and IntelXe Manager noticed one consequence, the system-volume copy that is
gone (`Health.swift` `ssv-gone`). This note designs a guard: the Manager warns before an update the driver does not
support, prepares a one-shot check for one it does, and that check repairs what it can at the first start of the new
macOS.

NullMoth's 1401 app has an "OS update guard" (`mac/Resources/nullmoth-setup.sh`, `--update prepare/finish`,
`com.nullmoth.osupdate`). It was read for ideas only (PolyForm Noncommercial); no code comes from it. Its approach:
park the driver with a boot-arg before a major update, a LaunchDaemon on the new macOS that rebuilds the kernel
collection, reinstalls and un-parks, a bounded number of tries, an expiry for a preparation that never saw an update,
and a log. Section 2 explains why this stack does not park; the rest (one-shot daemon, bounded tries, expiry, log)
is the same idea.

## 1. What the stack needs across an update

| Part | Where it lives | Minor update (26.7.x → 26.7.y) | Major update (26 → 27) |
|---|---|---|---|
| `IntelXe.kext` | the EFI; OpenCore's `Kernel > Add` injects it into every boot, the installer's included | stays. Links against `com.apple.kpi.*` 10.0.0 and up (`kernel/IntelXe/build.py`), which every newer kernel exports | stays and is injected; `com.apple.kpi.unsupported` may differ: it may fail to link (OpenCore logs and skips it) or start |
| `IntelXeFB`, `NMXAccel`, `NMXAGDC` | `/Library/Extensions`, in the Auxiliary Kernel Collection that `install.sh` builds with `kmutil create -n aux` against the boot and system collections | the files stay. The update replaces the boot and system collections the AuxKC was linked against; whether the update rebuilds the AuxKC with our kexts in it (they were put there by `kmutil` with SIP relaxed, not through the approval database) was **not recorded** on the test machine. The guard checks that they load instead of assuming it | NMXAccel is built for macOS 26's IOAcceleratorFamily2: its vtable forwarding is generated from 26's binary (`nullmoth/kexts/NVRM/accel/gen_tahoe_fwd.py`, `tahoe_fwd.h`). On 27 it either fails to link (no accelerator) or links with wrong slots (a panic in the first accelerated minute). Without the accelerator WindowServer has no desktop on the Arc (ROADMAP, boot guard) |
| the Metal driver | `/Library/GPUBundles` (data volume) | stays and is expected to work (the plugin interface did not change within 26) | built against 26's private Metal driver interface: unknown |
| the system-volume copy (Safari on the GPU) | `/System/Library/Extensions/NVMTLDriver.bundle` (sealed system volume) | **gone**: the update replaces the snapshot. Installing it again needs `SecureBootModel Disabled` and makes a new snapshot: a user decision (`ssv-install.sh --apply`) | gone |
| boot-args, `csr-active-config` | OpenCore's `config.plist` (`NVRAM > Add` and `Delete`) | stay | stay |
| the driver's NVRAM settings (`intelxe-*`, `intelxefb-*`) | NVRAM | stay (an update does not reset NVRAM; OpenCore's Reset NVRAM does) | stay |
| boot guard daemon (`guard-clear.sh`) | `/Library/LaunchDaemons` | stays | stays |
| `HybridPM.kext` | the EFI | stays; if the update changed the XCPM routine it corrects, it stands aside by itself (guide, route 3) | Lilu's range ends at Tahoe (`kernel/HybridPM/HybridPM.cpp`): it does not start |
| Zink, the Vulkan provider | `/Library/IntelXe` | stay | built against 26's frameworks: unknown |

So a minor update needs at most: the AuxKC rebuilt (`install.sh --apply`, which also puts back anything else that
went missing) and a restart, and the system-volume copy installed again if it was there. A major update the release
does not support cannot be repaired by reinstalling; it needs a release built for it.

## 2. Is parking needed? No

Parking means: before the update, make the driver not load (NullMoth writes `-nvoff` into the boot-args of the EFI's
`config.plist`), and turn it back on once the new macOS is set up. For this stack:

1. **A boot-arg cannot be set from macOS here.** Stage 2 of the install guide puts `boot-args` and
   `csr-active-config` in OpenCore's `NVRAM > Delete`, so OpenCore writes the config's values at every boot; an
   `nvram boot-args=...` from macOS is gone at the next start. Parking by boot-arg is an edit of the EFI's
   `config.plist` (efi.sh), before and after the update, on an EFI that may not be mounted at either moment.
2. **Parking costs the desktop.** On macOS 26 WindowServer has no desktop on the Arc without the accelerator (a held
   boot stays at the Apple logo: ROADMAP "Boot guard", README-INSTALL "If it does not come up"). The Arc has no Apple
   driver to fall back to. A parked first boot of the new macOS is certainly dark; an unparked one of a minor update
   is expected to work. For the common case parking is strictly worse.
3. **The kexts on an unknown macOS.** None of them checks the macOS version (no `version_major` or `osrelease` test
   in `kernel/IntelXe`, `kernel/IntelXeFB`; the OSBundleLibraries ask for `com.apple.kpi.*` 8.0 or 10.0 and newer).
   They load wherever their symbols resolve; what can go wrong is NMXAccel on a new major version (section 1).
4. **The boot guard already bounds a crash loop.** IntelXeFB counts accelerated boots that end inside their first
   minute (`intelxe-guard`): after two the next boots arm NMXAccel's safe settings, after four acceleration is held
   (`intelxe-accel-off`) until cleared from the Manager, over SSH (`sudo nvram intelxe-accel-off=ok`) or by Reset
   NVRAM in the picker. A new macOS that crashes the accelerator ends in a held, dark but running system, the same
   end state as parking, after at most four boots.
5. **What parking would add on a major update**: up to four panicking boots fewer. It would not give a desktop.

Decision: no parking. Instead:

- **Before**: warn about an offered update the installed release does not support (the Overview page, a banner, the
  check at login). The advice is to wait for a release; the guide's way back after a major update is Time Machine.
- **After**: check, and repair what reinstalling repairs (section 4).
- **The boot guard after an update**: the update's own restarts can end boots inside their first minute (a
  shutdown before the desktop was steady leaves `intelxe-guard` set). If the guard holds acceleration after the
  update, it was clear when the update was prepared, no kernel panic report was written since, and this is the first
  check after the update, the daemon clears it once (`intelxe-accel-off=ok`) and restarts. A panic report, or a
  second time, leaves it to the user.
- **The one real parking knob**, for whoever must run an unsupported major version anyway (with another GPU for the
  desktop): `MaxKernel` on IntelXe.kext's `Kernel > Add` entry (`25.99.99` keeps it out of Darwin 26 = macOS 27),
  and `install.sh --uninstall` for the /Library part. An EFI edit; the guard does not make it.

## 3. Detecting a pending and a finished update

| What | How | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| updates on offer | Software Update's record `/Library/Preferences/com.apple.SoftwareUpdate.plist`: `RecommendedUpdates` items with `Display Name`, `Display Version`, `Identifier` (`MSU_UPDATE_<build>_patch_<version>_<minor\|major>`), `MobileSoftwareUpdate`; `AutomaticallyInstallMacOSUpdates`. World-readable, written by softwareupdated's background scan. Seen on the development Mac (macOS 27.0.1): `MSU_UPDATE_26B131_patch_27.2.1_minor` with `Display Version` 27.2.1 | no network, no root, instant |
| updates on offer, now | `softwareupdate --list` (`* Label: macOS Tahoe 26.7.2-25H123` / `Title: ..., Version: 26.7.2, ...`): the "Check now" button | asks Apple's catalog: tens of seconds |
| an update happened | `ProductBuildVersion` in `/System/Library/CoreServices/SystemVersion.plist` against the build the preparation recorded (the daemon), or `kern.osversion` against the build the Manager saw at its last start (`lastSeenMacOSBuild`) | instant |
| an update is downloaded and staged | **not detectable without private APIs.** The download and preparation state belongs to MobileSoftwareUpdate (`/System/Library/AssetsV2/com_apple_MobileAsset_MacSoftwareUpdate/*.xml` lists the offered assets, not whether one is staged; `/System/Volumes/Update` holds the preparation in root-only places). The Manager therefore says "ready to install", not "downloaded" | |

Any build change counts as an update (a security response that changes the build too). The record says
`_major`/`_minor`; the guard does not rely on it and compares major version numbers itself.

## 4. The guard

### 4.1 Which macOS versions a release supports

`data/platforms.json` has no macOS list (it lists PCI devices and features); the app's only list is
`packageSuffix` (26 and 15). The authority is the package that gets installed, so `install.sh` answers:
`install.sh --supports-macos VERSION` prints `ok`, `untested` or `no`, from the same `macos_support` function its
`check` uses (Tahoe package: 26.7.x ok, another 26.x untested, anything else no; Sequoia package: 15.x ok), and
`--status` adds `macos_support=` for the running macOS. Packages before this branch (0.1.4) do not have it: their
own major version (`package_macos`) is supported, nothing else. The Manager (`macOSSupport`) and the daemon
(`support`) use the same rule. `untested` is treated as supported (install.sh itself only warns).

### 4.2 Before: Prepare

The Overview page's *macOS updates* section lists the offered updates with the verdict for each. **Prepare** (a
supported update, the installed release's package chosen on the Driver page) runs
`osupdate-guard.sh --prepare PACKAGE TARGET` as root through the password dialog (the app's usual path, no helper
tool). It:

1. checks the package against its `SHA256SUMS` and that it is the installed release (`installed-version`);
2. copies it to `/Library/Application Support/intel-gpu-macos-driver/osupdate/package`, root-owned: the daemon runs
   as root and must not run a script from the user's downloads folder, which the user (or anything running as the
   user) can change; the copy is checked against `SHA256SUMS` again before it is used;
3. copies the guard script itself next to it (the app may move or be replaced before the update);
4. records the state (`state`): versions, build, target, package version and macOS, the `restart` choice, and
   `--check` as it is now (kexts loaded, AuxKC, Metal driver, system-volume copy, boot guard), prefixed `before_`;
5. writes `/Library/LaunchDaemons/io.github.yusufklncc.intelxe.osupdate.plist` (`RunAtLoad`, `/bin/bash
   <kept script> --finish`), checked with `plutil -lint`; a file launchd could not read would leave a preparation
   that never runs, so then nothing is prepared.

The daemon is not loaded now: launchd loads it at the next start. An unsupported target can still be prepared (the
log notes it); the daemon then only reports. **Cancel the preparation** (`--cancel`) removes the daemon, the record
and the kept copy.

### 4.3 After: the daemon, once per start until it is done

| Situation | What it does | Result | Daemon |
|---|---|---|---|
| the build is the recorded one | logs "waiting" | – | stays |
| the same, 14 days after the preparation | gives up waiting | `expired` | removed |
| a new build: the count of checks goes up; the AuxKC's kexts get up to 90 s to load | `--check` into the log | | |
| the release does not support the new macOS | installs nothing | `unsupported` | removed |
| IntelXe.kext (from the EFI) is not loaded | installs nothing (the /Library kexts would have nothing to attach to) | `efi-kext` | removed |
| the boot guard holds acceleration, it was clear before, no panic report since the preparation, first check | `nvram intelxe-accel-off=ok intelxe-guard=ok` (both since the held-display branch: [`DESIGN-boot-guard-held-display.md`](DESIGN-boot-guard-held-display.md)) | `guard-cleared` | stays (checks again) |
| a kext installed but not loaded, the Metal driver missing, or installed files that differ from the package | checks the kept package's `SHA256SUMS` (else `refused`, removed), `install.sh --apply` (backs up, copies, rebuilds the AuxKC) | `repaired` | stays (checks again) |
| `--apply` failed | | `retrying`; `gave-up` at the third | stays; removed |
| still not loaded at the fourth check | | `gave-up` | removed |
| everything loads | notes a system-volume copy that is gone, a guard that holds after a panic | `ok` | removed |

After `repaired` or `guard-cleared` at the first check it restarts once by itself (`shutdown -r +1`), unless the
preparation said `--no-restart` (the Overview page's switch, on by default: without the AuxKC's kexts the Arc may
show no desktop to restart from). Bounds: at most three installs, one automatic restart, one guard clear. When it
is done it removes the LaunchDaemon file, the record and the kept package; `result` and `osupdate.log` stay. It never
touches the EFI.

### 4.4 After, without a preparation

The Manager remembers the build it saw at its last start. When it starts on another build that no daemon result
covers, the *macOS updates* section says so and shows `osupdate-guard.sh --check` (no root): kexts installed but not
loaded, the Metal driver missing, IntelXe.kext not loaded, the boot guard. When something is missing and the chosen
package supports the macOS, its button runs the Driver page's *Install this package*. A new health check,
`kexts-not-loaded` (IntelXeFB.kext in /Library/Extensions, IntelXe loaded, IntelXeFB not), puts the same thing in a
banner and in the dialog of the optional check at login. `ssv-gone` already covered the system-volume copy.

### 4.5 What the user sees

- The Overview page, *macOS updates*: the last result (with *Done*), the system-volume copy that went with the
  update (*Open the Driver page*), the preparation (*Cancel the preparation*), the offered updates with their
  verdict, *Prepare…*, the restart switch, *Check now*, and a note when Software Update installs updates by itself.
- Banners and the check at login (`healthIssues`): `osupdate-unsupported` (an offered update of another major
  version than the running one; key: its version, so a dismissal holds until another is offered), `osupdate-result`
  (a result that needs the user: `unsupported`, `efi-kext`, `gave-up`, `refused`, `retrying`), `kexts-not-loaded`.
- The Report page: `collect-macos.sh` adds `driver/osupdate-state.txt` (record, result, tries, daemon) and
  `logs/osupdate.log` (its last 400 lines).

## 5. Tests

- `app/tests/test-osupdate-guard.sh` (89 checks, about 15 s, no root): the guard against a throwaway root, with a
  package made from `release/templates/install.sh` (paths under the throwaway root, root and kmutil stubbed as
  `release/test-install-flow.sh` does) and stubs for `kmutil`, `nvram` and `shutdown`. It covers
  `install.sh --supports-macos` and `--status`; `--check`; Prepare refused without an installed driver, without a
  package, with another release's package, with a damaged one, and outside the test root without root; the record,
  the plist (`plutil -lint`), the kept copies; waiting and expiry; a minor update with everything loaded (nothing
  installed); one that lost the AuxKC and the system-volume copy (repaired, one restart, `ok` and `ssv=gone` after
  it); `--no-restart`; kexts that never load (three tries, one restart, `gave-up`); an unsupported major version
  (nothing installed, no restart); IntelXe.kext missing; the boot guard after the update with and without a panic
  report; a damaged kept package; `--apply` failing (retrying, gave-up); cancel; and a 0.1.4 package (from git
  history) without `--supports-macos`.
- `release/test-install-flow.sh` still passes with the changed `install.sh`.
- `IntelXeManager --selftest`: Software Update's record and `softwareupdate --list` parsed, support by major version,
  the result texts, `--status` read from the carried script; with a package, `--supports-macos` through the app.
  `--snapshot` adds `system-osupdate.png` (the Overview page with an offered supported update, an unsupported one and
  a result).

## 6. What needs a real update or the test machine

Not tested without one: the daemon at the first start of a really updated macOS (launchd loading it, the kexts'
load timing against the 90 s wait, `kmutil` at that moment), whether a minor update keeps our kexts in the AuxKC by
itself (the answer decides how often the repair runs), `install.sh --apply` from the daemon with no user logged in,
the automatic restart, the guard clear after real update restarts, Software Update's record on macOS 26 (it was read
on 27), the password dialog, and the banners and login dialog on the test machine. The next macOS 26.7.x update on
the test machine is the test: prepare it from the Manager, update, and read `osupdate.log`.

## 7. Files

`app/Resources/osupdate-guard.sh` (the guard), `app/Sources/OSUpdate.swift` (detection, verdicts, the Overview
section), `app/Sources/Health.swift` (`kexts-not-loaded`, `osUpdateIssues`), `app/Sources/Views.swift` (state,
refresh, banner fixes), `release/templates/install.sh` (`--supports-macos`, `macos_support=`),
`tools/report/collect-macos.sh` (the guard's state and log), `app/tests/test-osupdate-guard.sh`.
